They're based on assumptions discussed later on. These equations aren't an original contribution but rather a reference guide for those working with simplified numerical models of groundwater flow.

I began with Darcy's Law, revisiting the conservation equation for vertical averaging in groundwater flow. Following that, I explored approaches for numerically solving the flow equation. Then, I considered scenarios where the hydraulic conductivity varies solely with depth, simplifying the steady-state flow equation in these cases. Lastly, there's a brief examination of the transient flow scenario. 

It's worth noting that these equations don't account for factors like vertical leakage between aquifers and the effects of gravity on flow. Additionally, they don't account for changes in hydraulic conductivity beyond depth and the effects of pumping and recharge. These assumptions lead to simplified equations that would be inadequate for complex projects. 

Finally, there's a brief discussion on how to extend these equations to represent multi-layered aquifers. 

I hope these notes serve their intended purpose and are helpful to others working on similar projects. If you spot any errors, please don't hesitate to contact me. I'd be more than grateful if you could aid in improving these notes or contribute to their improvement in any way. 

## Darcy's Law

Darcy's Law describes the velocity of groundwater as a function of hydraulic conductivity (K), head (h), and viscosity (μ). It's typically written as:

V = -K/μ * ∂/∂x (ρgh + p)

Assuming constant viscosity, it simplifies to:

V = -K/ρ * ∂/∂x (gh + p)

It's commonly seen in the literature as:

V = -K * �partial head/�partial x

Where the head is represented as h + p/ρg.

## Conservation Equation for Vertical Averaging

The conservation equation for vertical averaging is:

0 = ∫[from the bottom of the aquifer to the top of the aquifer] (v_{in} - v_{out}) dz

It can be written as:

0 = ∫[from the bottom of the aquifer to the top of the aquifer] (V_{in} - V_{out}) dz

It simplifies to:

0 = (Q_{in} - Q_{out})/A

Where Q represents flow

While this feedback has some value, it can lead students to focus on irrelevant test cases and neglect others. As a result, the instructional focus shifts from grasping the subject matter to the mere completion of test cases, rather than their effective selection. Moreover, this approach only informs students of their mistakes after completing the testing activity, rather than teaching them how to incorporate conceptual coverage into their testing strategy. To address these issues, we have developed a novel method for integrating testing coverage into the teaching of software testing, enabled by modern educational tools. This approach prioritizes subject matter understanding and encourages selected test cases. Notably, the test conceptual coverage method demonstrated a 22% and 15% greater improvement in the understanding of software testing among novice and experienced students, respectively. The empirical investigation's findings can guide instructors in teaching students to effectively select test cases and incorporate conceptual coverage into their testing strategy. Research into remote epitaxy using monolayer graphene as a substrate has yielded encouraging results, yet significant hurdles remain to be overcome before achieving device-quality materials through this process. A crucial step in perfecting remote epitaxy involves the development of an in-depth understanding of how the epitaxial relationship between films and substrates operates. This study investigated the epitaxy of the Heusler alloy Ni$_2$MnSn (NMT) on monolayer graphene/sapphire, an ideal model system due to its minimal epitaxial constraints. Analysis of the epitaxial relationship between NMT and graphene revealed that ultra-vacuum deposition results in random NMT crystal orientations, whereas molecular beam epitaxy yields NMT films with a balance of epitaxial relationship, likely thanks to particle beam-induced heating. Using a balance of particle beam intensity and substrate temperature, we achieved NMT films with an optimal epitaxial relationship. Importantly, our findings also suggest that epitaxial relationship can be fine-tuned by adjusting particle beam intensity, opening up possibilities for the creation of quantum devices utilizing the unique properties of NMT without the need for lattice matching. Finally, comparison of NMT remote epitaxy on graphene with van der Waals epitaxy on hexagonal boron nitride/sapphire and pinhole epitaxy on GaN/sapphire highlights the unique characteristics of each method, paving the way for the development of novel hetero-epitaxial films featuring NMT, a material with significant data-storage and spintronics potential. Additionally, these studies provide insights into the mechanisms underlying NMT epitaxy, including an unexpected correlation between NMT epitaxial relationship and van der Waals epitaxy. Further work using monolayer NMT and incorporating other Heusler materials, such as Mn$_2$FeSn and NiFeCo, may further expand the horizons of remote epitaxy, ultimately enabling the fabrication of high-performance spintronics devices through this process. Lastly, our studies on NMT have also established a basis for exploring other Heusler materials and epitaxial relationships in this series of research. This research examines profit-sharing agreements between a single Content Provider and multiple Internet Service Providers, with the Content Provider agreeing to split profits in exchange for enhanced service quality by the ISPs. To model these negotiations, we use a Stackelberg game, where the Content Provider decides the distribution of its profits and the ISPs determine their level of investment effort, while in another scenario, we look into how Content Providers and ISPs collaborate, with ISPs deciding on how to split the profits fairly through a Nash Bargaining model, resulting in improved outcomes for all parties. Numerical findings show the existence of unique equilibria in both scenarios, with specific parameters and models supporting our analysis. This study ultimately contributes to the understanding of how Content Providers and ISPs can mutually benefit from joint profits in a distributed environment. Interestingly, results show that when using the Nash model, a fair split of 0.5 exists for all profits, whereas the Stackelberg model requires a varying split of profits (.25 for the Content Provider and.75 for the ISPs), which might pose challenges in real-world applications where agreements are negotiated individually. This study follows up on previous works on profit-sharing and enhances the understanding of scenarios where Content Providers and ISPs collaborate. Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) and was tested on noisy recordings obtained from multiple stethoscopes, demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed technique achieves the best results across a wide range of recording conditions and environments, indicating its potential for low-cost implementation.  The findings provide a framework for creating cardiac auscultation systems capable of accurately diagnosing conditions even in noisy environments using low-cost devices.  The research offers a theoretical basis for designing effective feature sets that can enhance the performance of cardiac auscultation systems through feature transformation.  Additionally, a comparative study of various deep learning architectures is conducted, including the evaluation of a Simple Neural Network (SNN), a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and a ResNet, which ultimately leads to the determination of the optimal architecture for cardiac auscultation sound analysis.  Based on these outcomes, the development of low-cost, portable systems for diagnosing cardiac conditions using cardiac auscultation sounds that can operate effectively in noisy environments using standard equipment such as smartphones becomes feasible.  The research provides a foundation for creating such systems capable of diagnosing conditions such as heart failures and cardiomyopathies. The dataset contains recordings affected by background noise and variability of recording devices, as well as normal and abnormal sound patterns.  The recordings were obtained using standard equipment for cardiac auscultation and are represented in the frequency domain.

This study offers the first empirical evaluation of the influence of auction format integrity on bidding tactics and outcome profitability. Through controlled lab experiments where auction participants can view other bidders' auction history, we examine whether a credible auction environment (where auction results are consistently paid for) affects bidding in comparison to a non-credible one (where auction participants may be charged more than they win). Our findings indicate that a credible auction leads to more aggressive bidding and greater auction profits. Notably, our study also reveals that a non-credible auction scenario results in short-term monetary gains among bidders. Building on these findings, we propose an explanation grounded in psychological theories of loss aversion and the significance of integrity in building trust among auction participants. Ultimately, our study contributes to the understanding of the effectiveness of one-shot auctions in facilitating trustworthy interactions among strangers. 

Keywords: Credibility in auctions, Second-price auctions, Experimental economics, Bidding tactics, Auction profits, Trustworthiness.

Physicians' written assessments and interviews with patients, stored as unstructured clinical text notes (CTNs), have been analyzed by recent studies using machine learning techniques to forecast diagnoses based on CTNs, a task known as International Classification of Diseases (ICD) coding. Annotating medical data can be particularly labor-intensive due to the required level of specialization. This study presents an innovative approach to supplement a sparsely annotated collection of Icelandic CTNs using semi-self-supervised machine-learned imputation. By initially training a neural network on a small number of annotated CTNs, the model extracts clinical characteristics from un-annotated CTNs, generating around a thousand potential clinical feature answers for physicians to consult during patient evaluations. These features are then applied to develop a diagnosis classifier for specific medical conditions. An assessment was conducted on this augmentation technique across various degrees of annotation sparsity and compared against alternative data augmentation methods. As a result, the models learned from the feature-rich CTNs delivered more accurate predictions of medical conditions based on CTNs with the highest clinical relevance, while also showing improved performance with increasing degrees of annotation sparsity. Notably, the models trained on our augmentation technique outperformed previous models trained on smaller, independently-annotated patient datasets. An evaluation was conducted using three physicians to forecast diagnoses based on CTNs, showing our semi-self-supervised approach enabled more accurate predictions, higher clinical relevance, and improved medical condition coverage compared to previous studies on this dataset. The code for our data augmentation technique has been made open-source on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/spliorg/hl2_ICD_Coding. Additionally, the code has been shared on GitHub according to the guidelines established by the Neuromorphics Foundation. Please feel free to contact the corresponding author at [jarni@spli.org](jarni@spli.org) for more information on this project, including access to our training data. Let $R$ be a polynomial ring in $n$ variables over a field $k$. A monomial ideal $I$ within this ring is considered. This paper explores almost Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes and provides specific classifications for certain types of ideals, including polymatroidal Veronese type and transversal polymatroidal ideals, along with illustrative examples. Additionally, it discusses the relationship between minimal free resolutions of these ideals and their linear strand. Finally, some conclusions regarding Lyubeznik numbers, Hilbert functions, and projective invariants are drawn. This research was initially presented at the 12th Conference on Commutative Algebra and Algebraic Geometry, held at the University of Kansas.

Due to the diverse applications of machine learning, its ability to identify patterns in datasets is well-established, albeit limited by the rapid growth of computation time with dataset size. A shift towards quantum computing could potentially resolve this limitation, providing an alternative to current statistical models. We develop and test a quantum equivalent to the K-means clustering method on superconducting qubits, contrasting it to a previously implemented quantum support vector machine. Results indicate that our algorithm matches classical K-means performance in both clustering and classification tasks, achieving an impressive speedup due to a lower asymptotic complexity of $O(N^3)$ compared to $O(N^5)$ with existing methods. Additionally, we leverage this quantum clustering method to efficiently train a quantum neural network and achieve notable reductions in training time and circuit depth. This work lays the groundwork for future applications of quantum machine learning in data analysis. A detailed description of the experiments and measurements has been made publicly available. Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in image-based inverse problems due to its potential to enhance traditional optimization-based methods and offer self-supervision for learning-based approaches, particularly those lacking ground truth-annotated training data. However, existing differentiable renderers are either limited by their failure to account for light source visibility, resulting in inaccurately rendered shadows, or hindered by slow computation, preventing them from efficiently training deep models. To address these issues, we introduce an accurate yet high-performance approach that leverages spherical harmonics approximations to model scene illumination and visibility, using spherical approximations for occluding surfaces to significantly speed up shadow computation compared to ray tracing-based methods. By formulating this approach as a differentiable system, we can efficiently utilize analysis-by-synthesis optimization to recover texture, illumination, rigid pose, and geometric deformations from images. Notably, our method excels in handling complex poses, geometric deformations, and varied lighting environments. Furthermore, we demonstrate its ability to offer interpretability and denoising capabilities, showcasing its potential as a differentiable solver for a wide range of image-based inverse problems. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ivs-rwth/efficientShadows.ystems.

This collaborative approach in visual analytics aims to facilitate seamless interaction between humans and machines, according to established standards and best practices. Multiple frameworks strive to achieve this level of collaboration, but often fail to consider essential factors, resulting in systems that are impossible to use or unreliable. To address this, we present Lotse, a practical framework for creating intelligent support systems that learn and adapt to their users' skills and working methods. It provides a unified structure for implementing guidance based on expertise and experience, across various interaction forms, and is capable of improving interaction quality over time. Lotse's unique features and benefits are showcased through a practical application involving a collaborative visual analysis process. Empirical testing validates its effectiveness and usability, and the framework is now available under an open-source license on GitHub. We envision Lotse as a versatile tool for developing intelligent support systems in a range of application areas, including but not limited to, visual analytics, programming, and text editing. It has the potential to revolutionize the creation of support systems in these fields. In the future, we plan to expand Lotse to encompass more sophisticated forms of guidance, like multi-strategic guidance, and apply it to complex tasks, such as full-text programming. By combining Lotse with strategic expertise, we believe we can create innovative, intelligent tools that learn and adapt to their environment, and ultimately improve overall performance. Furthermore, this combination can be utilized to study and analyze various methods for providing guidance, particularly how expert strategies are influenced by level of knowledge and experience, and how these strategies can be leveraged to create more informative insights, and ultimately, more intelligent support systems. It also enables us to investigate how expert strategies can be utilized to create intelligent support systems, and whether and how these support systems can be utilized to analyze and understand the core elements of expert knowledge, ultimately leading to a deeper understanding of how expertise is developed and maintained. This, in turn, can lead to more informative and detailed prescriptions for creating systems that are tailored to the task at hand. This includes, but is not limited to, guidance, full-fidelity reproduction, and structured code generation. Ultimately, the fundamental concepts underlying Lotse, and its capacity to learn and adapt, can lead to a significant advancement in the study of complex systems, and provide a model for systematic analysis and understanding of expert knowledge, and its potential to be automated. In the long term, we intend for Lotse to embody a learning paradigm in which support systems evolve alongside their users, and continually improve their performance through shared learning. We've developed an innovative approach for designing stellarators with considerable versatility. Flexibility in this context refers to the range of rotational transform values the stellarator's magnetic axis can accommodate without compromising its quasisymmetry properties. Our method enhances design flexibility by taking into account coil placement during the modular coil design process, leveraging planar control coils and integrability objectives to improve quasisymmetry and nested flux surface volume. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by optimizing a coil set inspired by NCSX design, which allows for a range of rotational transform values between 0.3 and 0.6. Additionally, our design retains a strong connection between the magnetic axis and the stellarator's hollow volume, which is crucial for optimal plasma confinement. We successfully demonstrated that our stellarator design can accommodate a range of internal transport barriers and natural confinement regimes similar to those found in tokomaks. Our research indicates that, in terms of design complexity, variations of rotational transform are tied to differences in planar currents, which can be achieved through minor adjustments to the stellarator's inner volume. Consequently, we contend that design options exist that can strike an optimal balance between flexibility, hollow volume, and quasisymmetry, aiding in the development of a more versatile stellarator design. Furthermore, our research is transferable to other stellarator designs, which can be modified using our techniques to exhibit enhanced flexibility. Ultimately, our findings underscore the potential for stellarators to surpass tokomaks in terms of achieved rotational transform values, which holds significant potential for enhanced fusion performance. Achieving uniform temperature distribution within catalytic fixed bed reactors is critical, yet often hindered by hot spots caused by fluid dynamics irregularities, heat transfer variations, and catalyst particle size disparities. Using rapid Magnetic Resonance Imaging, we studied temperature distribution in a gas-solid fixed bed reactor at different flow rates, gas temperatures, and particle sizes. The results showed temperature inhomogeneities are more pronounced at lower flow rates and larger particle sizes. The correlation between temperature and fluid velocity and particle size is further analyzed. The implementation of RMS-based temperature fluctuation measurement enables the evaluation of thermal non-equilibrium between gas and solids, providing valuable insight for scaling up the process. Our study suggests using larger particles could minimize temperature hotspots, while also potentially increasing reactor efficiency by allowing higher conversion rates. The technique has the potential to be a vital tool for optimizing fixed bed reactor operations and understanding related microfluidic heat transfer phenomena. A simplified computational model is also proposed to explain the temperature distribution pattern observed in the study. The temperature distribution pattern can be accurately predicted using the model, demonstrating a strong relationship between the mean temperature and the mean fluid velocity, and the particle size, with a prediction accuracy of 0.001 for the mean temperature and 0.004 for the RMS temperature fluctuation. The model can be further applied to clarify the underlying physics of the temperature distribution in gas-solid non-equilibrium systems, and has the potential for a wider range of applications including heat transfer, microfluidics, and pharmacology. Based on this research, we suggest several future studies, such as investigating the effect of particle size on flow patterns and heat transfer, and exploring the application of this imaging technique to clarify the underlying mechanisms in thermally non-equilibrium systems. Additionally, we propose utilizing this technology to study the role of fluid dynamics in heat transfer and other gas-solid interactions, and suggest conducting similar experiments with a wider range of particle sizes, as well as examining the connection between temperature fluctuations and fluid velocity. The study also identifies potential future research areas, such as employing this technique to examine the link between fluid dynamics and heat transfer and other gas-solid interactions, and proposes conducting further experiments with a broader selection of particle sizes, with a particular focus on how temperature fluctuations correlate with fluid velocity. The research outlines its achievements, including characterizing temperature distribution in a fixed bed system through MRI, and presents a simplified model to explain the observed temperature variations, with the potential for this technique to be a key tool in understanding gas-solid heat transfer phenomena. Within a cellular environment, proteins and nucleic acids autonomously separate, resulting in the spontaneous formation of membraneless droplets. This process underlies the development of numerous sub-cellular compartments. In a model system designed to replicate this phenomenon, proteins with interacting properties and RNA molecules are isolated within droplets formed from concentrated solutions. Introducing common components to the system, either as droplet contents or surface residues, enhances droplet interaction and results in the coassembly of complexes containing both proteins and RNA. The coassembly is dictated by protein-RNA interactions that surpass individual protein-protein and RNA-RNA interactions. The resulting droplets display increased stability and resistance to solute concentrations. Additionally, introducing a large number of shared components leads to the formation of connected networks bridging protein and RNA compartments within the droplets. Such coassembly patterns are comparable to those observed in fundamental cellular structures, such as P bodies and stress granules. Observations indicate that, even in isolated systems, self-assembled compartments can exhibit intricate relationships reminiscent of core components, implying a complex interplay between proteins and nucleic acids in membraneless compartments. Furthermore, this research suggests a mechanism for the self-assembly of cells into stable compartments through shared components, potentially regulated by cellular signals. Such a mechanism may also underlie associated cellular pathways, and our study provides a starting point for exploring this possibility. Lastly, our research offers a practical approach for studying relationships between proteins and nucleic acids within cellular microdomains and their implications for understanding cellular homeostasis and associated diseases. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is designed to simulate an unknown, feature-rich 3D world, prompting an agent to navigate and gather information about the environment and its tasks, all while facing common challenges such as partial observability, unpredictable dynamics, and competing rewards. The open-source platform, powered by C#, is specifically tailored for evaluation in lifelong learning assessments, offering a range of beneficial characteristics, including adjustable learning rates, distinct task durations, and a range of reward structures. In medical contexts, diverse information often arises from various sources, which when combined enables more precise diagnosis. Doctors might initially learn about a patient's condition through spoken descriptions or written records, later consulting imaging or laboratory test data. Each source typically provides unique diagnostic information, highlighting the importance of data fusion in medical diagnosis. This study combines multiple information types (spoken, written, image-based) to improve the accuracy of eye condition classifications. We began by collecting and compiling a dataset of spoken English descriptions, corresponding written descriptions, and expert annotations for certain eye conditions. We developed and tested classification models that integrated these information types, ultimately finding that their combination yielded superior diagnostic accuracy rates of 92% for glaucoma and 87.5% for retinal conditions. Notably, these results were achieved through models trained on a relatively small dataset, which didn't receive expert training on the eye conditions in question. Instead, the models learned to compensate for the limited training data by processing and combining multiple information types. This research lays the groundwork for developing accurate, deep-learning based diagnostic tools, which like human medicine, can learn and improve over time even with sparse training data, particularly in complex fields like ophthalmology. We're making our information-rich dataset available to the public to support the development of advanced medical diagnostic tools. Our code is also publicly accessible, enabling other researchers to build upon our work and expand it with their own information types, ensuring a robust, publicly accessible dataset can be developed to support the advancement of medical diagnostics. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with and without severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this method demonstrated comparable performance. Additionally, the most important features derived from this analysis align with established medical knowledge, further validating the approach. While promising, this work is hindered by limited data and the need for further medical validation. Subsequent studies will investigate the proposed features in prospective experiments. It is anticipated that these results will contribute to the development of a low-cost, high-transparency tool for estimating the risk of severe COVID-19 symptoms from X-ray images. As a starting point, this work seeks to expand the scope of potential features from image data to include clinical data, potentially offering a more comprehensive understanding of patients' medical condition. By combining both image and clinical data, a more detailed and nuanced characterization of high-risk patients may be possible, offering substantial value in informing medical decisions during the current pandemic and beyond. Lastly, it is worth noting that while the proposed method exhibits notable performance, it fails to achieve high accuracy compared to more complex neural networks incorporating large sets of features. As such, this work can be viewed as an exploratory study aimed at extracting and interpreting crucial image features, rather than a competing model for predictive tasks. Future developments may build upon these results, incorporating additional data and using more complex models to develop a more sophisticated risk assessment system. Finally, the code and pre-trained models accompanying this paper have been made publicly available on github.com/clinical-feature-learning. Additionally, the derived features and accompanying medical information have been uploaded to figshare.com. Furthermore, the related dataset containing clinical notes has been uploaded to t.co. Finally, the related dataset comprising ICU admission information has been uploaded to https://doi.org/10.17632/5z5hbt9y9k/v1.

If $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ are constant, we prove the existence of transmission eigenfunctions that become localized around the boundary of $\Omega$. Our results generalize the recent studies in the mentioned literature and also illustrate the influence of medium parameters $\sigma$ and $\mathbf{n}$ on the geometric patterns of transmission eigenfunctions via numerical experiments. To expand a dialogue system's capabilities and facilitate its practical use, discovering new intent categories from user inputs is essential but remains understudied. Current methods are often inefficient, inaccurate, and require extensive labeling. We address two key research questions for this challenge by proposing novel approaches: (1) developing a universal representation for user inputs and detected query representations to enhance intent discovery; (2) designing an unsupervised method to identify hidden intent patterns through context-aware similarity comparison. Our results show substantial improvements over the existing state-of-the-art approaches on three benchmark datasets, requiring significantly fewer annotations to match their performance. Moreover, our method excels in a real-world scenario, uncovering new intent categories relevant to patient care using unlabelled medical conversation data. The source code for this work is available at https://github.com/ghruo/NewID.

The classical universal bundle functor W mapping from the category of simplicial groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of simplicial groups in C, and this extension holds for simplicial algebras defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory. Furthermore, when C is a category of spaces, particularly in the senses of simplicial sets or topological spaces, the resulting monadic coproduct with respect to W is strictly universal. Using this, we establish that the homotopy category of simplicial groups in C is defined as a universal quotient of the category of simplicial groups in C by a subfunctor that characterizes homotopy equivalences, and similarly for classifying groups in the homotopy category of simplicial sets. Moreover, in these cases, the classical universal bundle functor S mapping from the homotopy category of simplicial groups in C to the homotopy category of simplicial sets is a left adjoint to a functor mapping from the homotopy category of simplicial groups in C to the homotopy category of simplicial sets that is defined as a composition of functors that identify homotopy equivalences in a group as being in a splitting. Finally, in these cases, the left adjoint to the universal bundle functor S exists and is part of an equivalence in adjunction with the universal bundle functor W. Additionally, we give experimental evidence supporting a conjecture that the left adjoint to the universal bundle functor W exists and is part of an equivalence in adjunction with the universal bundle functor S for simplicial groups defined by any Lawvere theory that includes group theory. This conjecture would imply that the homotopy category of simplicial groups in C is defined as a universal quotient of the category of simplicial groups in C by a funtor that characterizes homotopy equivalences. Finally, we establish that the classical universal bundle functor U mapping from the category of groups in C to the category of simplicial sets in C lifts to a monadic structure on the category of groups in C, and that this extension holds for any Lawvere theory, and that the resulting monadic coproduct with respect to U is strictly universal in categories of spaces. Using this, we establish that the homotopy category of groups in C is defined as a universal quotient of the category of groups in C by a funtor that characterizes homotopy

This study re-examines the Adler-Bobenko-Suris H2 equation. The equation has a direct linear relationship with the Cauchy matrix scheme variables S0,0 and S1,0. A detailed analysis is provided on the coupled system of these variables in terms of 3D consistency, Lax pair, bilinear form and continuum limits. The analysis reveals that the variable S1,0 itself adheres to a 9-point lattice equation and upon continuum limiting, it is related to the Lax pair's eigenfunction of the Korteweg-de Vries equation. An interesting feature observed is that the variable S1,0 can be expressed as the sum of two Lax pair's eigenfunctions, where one of the eigenfunctions belongs to a special case of the nonlinear Schrödinger equation's soliton solution. Moreover, the study shows that S1,0 itself directly translates to a soliton solution in the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, thereby indicating a new method of obtaining soliton solutions. An observation is also made regarding the connection between the nonlinear Schrödinger equation and the H2 equation, where it is noticed that S1,0's soliton solution does not actually solve the H2 equation's continuum limit, however it does conform to another continuum limit of a 9-point lattice equation. An interesting contrast is noted between this finding and a similar investigation on the Toda molecule equation. Additionally, an interaction move between two solitons in the nonlinear Schrödinger equation, where one soliton's characteristics are derived from S1,0, is presented and verified through direct computation using the Cauchy matrix scheme. The computation first applies a special 'interaction matrix' to transform the initial soliton into a desired soliton, where the 'interaction matrix' interestingly holds a special 'upper-triangle' property in this particular coordinate system. The study then verifies the result by breaking down the computation into a series of 'interaction elements', where the total effect of the 'interaction matrix' is achieved through the cumulative effect of all the 'interaction elements'. The study shows that the total effect notably doesn't follow the expected'reflection symmetry', instead it only adheres to a'reflection inverse' after the total cumulative computation has been performed. The study then presents a distinct 'interaction element' case where the 'interaction element' actually translates to a perfect square of a specific 'interaction constant'. The study then poses an open question whether this 'interaction constant' could hold

This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA introduces a novel sampling method that incorporates balanced negative proposals mimicking the frequency of hard positive samples. By doing so, the model focuses more on accurately classifying hard proposals while controlling false positive rates. Our experiments show substantial improvements over current leading methods in the synthetic and real-world datasets, MDP and VQA-VIPER. The code for this work can be found at https://github.com/SamAcosta95/SABRA. Furthermore, we introduce a new evaluation metric, $F_1$-norm, to compare models' performance across different frequency distributions, which can be accessed at https://github.com/SamAcosta95/FDKE. This metric provides a more comprehensive understanding of the model's capability in distinguishing hard and easy proposals. By open-sourcing our code, we aim to facilitate the development of balanced models in computer vision, particularly for VRD. Additionally, we create a new dataset, HPS, containing 158K annotations with explicit frequency information, which can be accessed at https://github.com/SamAcosta95/HPS. The frequency information in HPS can be utilized by the computer vision community to develop and evaluate balanced models. Through our work, we aim to contribute to the advancement of VRD by addressing high false positive rates and frequency biases. A new measure, referred to as quantum correlation cost (QCC), quantifies the amount of quantum correlation employed in weak measurement procedures utilizing the trace norm. It's demonstrated that the QCC has a straightforward interpretation as the minimum amount of quantum resource required for weak measurement tasks and that it serves as a reliable indicator of quantum entanglement in certain scenarios. Furthermore, the QCC is shown to have a clear connection with resource theory-based approaches to studying quantum resource manipulation, specifically with the resource distance in the context of output classicality in weak measurement. It's established that the QCC is a more convenient and efficient measure to evaluate quantum resource for weak measurement compared to the resource distance. Lastly, a method using deformed logarithmic operators is proposed to effectively bound the QCC for a broad family of Markovian processes. This method exhibits better performance compared to previous studies. Our research not only delves into the properties of quantum correlation cost, as an independent measure, but also offers valuable insights into the intricate connections among quantum entanglement, nonclassicality, and other related concepts. Additionally, the QCC's simplicity and effectiveness make it a valuable tool for practical quantum information processing tasks. It's anticipated that the findings will contribute to the development of future research in quantum information technology by providing fresh perspectives on quantum correlation. Specifically, the QCC's versatile nature may find applications in studying the conversion and exchange of quantum information in weak measurement processes. It's further expected that the research will inspire investigations into resource theories of quantum information via the quantum correlation cost's distinctive properties and applications. Consequently, the study may pave the way for novel, practical realizations of quantum information processing by decomposing and analyzing the quantum correlation cost. As a result, the quantum correlation cost may offer valuable insights into the amount of quantum resource employed in weak measurement procedures and serve as a crucial indicator for evaluating quantum resource in such processes. It's further anticipated that the findings will promote the development of new, practical quantum information technologies by illustrating its equivalence to the quantum resource distance in certain contexts. It's concluded that the quantum correlation cost provides a concise and effective means to measure quantum resource and that it can be effectively bounded using the deformed logarithmic operator method. Artificial intelligence's interest in socially-aware agents is increasing. To address this, systems capable of deciphering diverse social interactions are needed. Understanding social relationships in a visual setting requires not only object recognition but also an in-depth comprehension of relationships and attributes within that scene. An explicit knowledge graph can be employed to model human connections and attributes, allowing for advanced reasoning. A novel neural network is introduced that can generate a structured graph of social relationships from an input image. This network, called the Social Relationship Graph Generation Network (SRG-GN), utilizes GRUs to iteratively refine social connection representations by combining visual scene and attribute context. By enabling message exchange between nodes in the graph, the network outperforms existing social relationship recognition methods. We showcase the efficacy of this model across three datasets: the OpenGRM-Dataset, the SocialX-Dataset, and the Flickr-Dataset. By comparing the network's performance on the OpenGRM-Dataset with state-of-the-art methods, it is evident that SRG-GN achieves superior results, specifically an 85% accuracy when evaluating relationship type and a 71% accuracy when evaluating attribute classification. Furthermore, the network demonstrates versatility through applications on the Flickr-Dataset and SocialX-Dataset. As a result, the SRG-GN model represents a significant advancement in social relationship recognition, effectively utilizing attributes and relationships to outperform existing methods. You can view the generated social relationship graphs produced by the SRG-GN model on our project website: https://srggn.net. Additionally, the accompanying code can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/sunghwanpyo/srggn. (On Google Drive: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1kxT0p0bH5kTLR7y4z4k)._

Capturing long-range relationships in scene understanding tasks is a crucial goal in computer vision. While CNNs excel in many vision tasks, they have limitations in modelling global, structured relationships due to their localized nature. A fully connected graph like the self-attention mechanism in Transformers is beneficial, but comes with prohibitively high computational costs. We propose a new graph neural network called dynamic graph message passing network that efficiently models long-range relationships by adaptively selecting relevant nodes in the graph for message passing, thereby reducing computational complexity compared to prior approaches. This allows us to design a self-attention module and a new Transformer-based backbone for image classification that outperforms state-of-the-art models on benchmark datasets. Moreover, we enhance this module to support semantic segmentation, object detection, and panoptic segmentation, achieving competitive results on benchmark datasets. A flexible and efficient implementation is provided on GitHub for reproducibility. A detailed breakdown of the code and model is available on GitHub: https://github.com/wu7120/dgmpn. This study is partially supported by CRCN grant 258812. The lead author's website is https://www.wangzhizhou.com/. (In English)

Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to a common operation called Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM) over integers. One efficient way to achieve this optimization is by replacing expensive generic multiplication with bit-shifts and additions in a multiplierless circuit. Our work advances the state-of-the-art in optimal MCM approaches based on Integer Linear Programming (ILP) and introduces a novel hardware cost model. This model counts one-bit adders, demonstrating a strong correlation with the number of LUTs required. Our proposed model can be used for automatic MCM code generation and demonstrates improved code quality when compared to existing methods. Additionally, we investigate various concepts related to optimal MCM, including circuit symmetries and the complexity of optimal solutions. Our research provides insights on the feasibility of solving large ILP problems and facilitates the development of near-optimal solutions based on heuristics. A set of experimental results shows the effectiveness of our proposed model in generating high-quality MCM code. Our model can be accessed through a public C++ API and used in other software tools for improved MCM code generation. A novel software tool, McMBuilder, is also provided for translating ILP constraints into actual MCM code and McMAnalyzer is used for analyzing the efficiency of existing MCM codes. Both tools are publicly available. Our research sets a new standard for measuring the hardware cost of MCM code and demonstrates the feasibility of building a customized hardware for a specific integer, which is shown on a Digilent Nano Board. Our work lays the foundation for a customized hardware for a specific integer and extends this concept to MCM codes. Also, our research applies our hardware cost model to several domains, such as embedded systems, digital signal processing, and machine learning, and shows the efficacy of our model in these domains. Furthermore, our research is the first to utilize the principle of symmetric hardware implementation in MCM codes. Also, our research utilises circuit compaction techniques to reduce the area of MCM circuits through circuit rearrangement. Additionally, our research introduces a novel concept called modular MCM, which is useful for a custom hardware for an arbitrary integer and extends this concept to MCM codes. Finally, our research sets a new standard for measuring the efficiency of MCM codes based on additive symmetries. Additionally, our research presents a novel additive compiler that transforms a MCM code with reflective symmetry into an additive MCM code with a reduced hardware cost. The intersection of quantum computing and deep neural networks has recently given rise to a growing research field, known as quantum deep learning. Despite previously being separate entities, advancements have revealed that quantum circuits share parallels with artificial neural networks, paving the way for widespread adoption. This paper delves into the foundational aspects and core principles of quantum deep learning, highlighting key breakthroughs along the way. It also explores the challenges inherent in quantum deep learning research from multiple viewpoints, followed by a discussion of prospective future directions and practical applications. Additionally, the appendix provides a comprehensive overview of relevant publications up to the manuscript submission date. This paper aims to serve as an entry point and reference for researchers interested in the field of quantum deep learning. Experimental evidence demonstrating the practical benefits of quantum circuits in machine learning is still lacking; hence, further research is needed to firmly establish the field of quantum deep learning. This paper assumes a basic understanding of quantum computing and neural networks, covering necessary background in Chapter 2. It then overviews quantum deep learning research in Chapter 3, before delving into issue-spotting and potential future directions in Chapter 4. Finally, the manuscript concludes in Chapter 5. This paper can be summarized into individual chapters for teaching quantum circuits and neural networks, as a quantum deep learning course. Additionally, the manuscript can be summarized without the assumption that the reader has knowledge in quantum computing and neural networks. Clearly, drawing parallels between quantum circuits and neural networks is problematic if the audiences lack the essential background. This paper can be summarized into two distinct versions: a comprehensive overview and a summary aimed at readers with prior knowledge of quantum circuits and neural networks. The quantum deep learning research field may benefit from distinguishing between various subfields, such as the quantum circuit model, the measurement-based model, and hybrid approaches. Similarly, researchers may also organize themselves into distinct groups based on the specific subfields within quantum deep learning. Moreover, the term "quantum deep learning" might not adequately capture the complexity and diversity within the field; hence, a broader term such as "quantum artificial intelligence" could be employed. This may also reflect how the field will evolve in the future. There is no consensus yet on how to encompass the diverse research areas within quantum deep learning. Therefore, this manuscript uses the term "quantum deep learning" to refer to a specific research field aligned with the measurement-based model. In contrast, artificial intelligence encompasses a broader range of research areas, including machine learning driven by data,, which might be more representative of the diverse research areas within quantum deep learning

In the near future, physicists anticipate that the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) will discover new physics. However, the specific characteristics and energy thresholds of this new physics remain unknown. It's probable that insights gleaned from LHC data will require supplementary information obtained from a lepton collider to conduct a thorough investigation. This text discusses the underlying principles, accelerator layout, and detector development for a high-energy Muon Collider as well as the difficulties inherent in the machine and its detector environment. It's also exploring innovative solutions to overcome these difficulties and compares the options for a high-energy Muon Collider to other possibilities, such as proton colliders. Ultimately, several construction timelines are possible, with the Muon Collider potentially being built in the mid-21st century. The text concludes by highlighting the urgent need for researchers to make a collective effort to advance the concept, addressing challenges critical to the advancement of particle physics. This presentation was initially an oral contribution to the 2022 Snowmass Topical Workshop on Future Collider Physics Research. This material is an expanded version of the corresponding talk.

Our research assesses whether the cosmic background of Hawking radiation from primordial black holes could be the source behind the observed excess radiowave signals. By assuming that dark matter exists entirely as these black holes, we calculated that the temperature resulting from Hawking radiation is negligible in comparison to the cosmic microwave background, primarily due to the low energy output of these events. Although radio signals have been detected within the 1-10 GHz frequency range and could be attributed to PMBs, our findings indicate that Hawking radiation from PBHs cannot be the underlying cause. This discrepancy is likely resolved by assuming that a portion of these black holes undergo accretion, emitting radiation across various spectra. This process could provide a potential explanation for the observed excess signals, suggesting a need for further investigation into this phenomenon. If Hawking radiation is to be detected, it's likely that a more extensive array such as the Square Kilometre Array will be required. Similarly, the Luhan Telescope is expected to play a crucial role in verifying the prediction for PBH-generated radiation. Both initiatives, however, would need to account for the growing contamination from civilisation noise in the relevant frequency range. This could be mitigated in part by the development of next-generation radio interferometers with the capability to reach up to 100,000 square kilometer in array size. Ultimately, the pursuit of this endeavor hinges on the resolution of the issue surrounding the existence of these black holes, particularly as related to the phenomenon of jet-induced reionisation. This area of research remains contentious, with a particular focus on the potential role of these black holes in the reionisation of the cosmos. If demonstrated, this evidence could not only validate the theory of these black holes as radiation sources but also reveal previously unexplored aspects of the universe's evolution. In contrast, a failure to support this theory would likely rule out Hawking radiation as the underlying cause of the observed signals, strengthening the case for PMBs in this context. Additionally, a demonstration of these black holes' role in the cosmos could potentially unlock significant advancements in fundamental research, encompassing topics such as dark matter and the primordial distribution of matter and radiation. This could be accomplished by detecting radiation generated from these black holes in the 1-10 Hz frequency range using the Luhan Telescope, an endeavor that is anticipated to be pivotal in resolving the underlying theory. Introducing the Virtual Secure Platform (VSP), a pioneering solution that brings together multi-opcode general-purpose sequential processing with Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to enable Secure Multi-Party Computation (SMPC) at a secure computing offloading level, such as cloud computing. The VSP safeguardingly shields both input data and function evaluations against adversaries in a secure computing offloading scenario like cloud computing. To enhance performance, our innovative VSP architecture features a five-stage pipeline design that increases circuit evaluation parallelism. Moreover, a custom-designed Instruction Set Architecture (ISA) was created to decrease processor gate count, accompanied by comprehensive toolchains allowing for arbitrary C program compilation into our custom ISA. To further boost performance, CMUX Memory-based ROM and RAM implementations over FHE were developed. Experimentation results confirm the effectiveness of the pipelined architecture and CMUX Memory approach in significantly accelerating VSP processing speed. We made the VSP source code available and achieved remarkable results, with each instruction taking under 1 second to complete, a substantial improvement over current existing processors over FHE. The VSP prototype has outperformed the best competing processor, executing nearly 1,600 times faster. Moreover, when comparing the entire processor pipelines, our VSP exhibited an impressive 66 times faster execution speed. To further validate the feasibility of applying the VSP in real-world scenarios, a cloud-based service utilizing VSP was developed, demonstrating the versatility of the Virtual Secure Platform. Researchers investigate polynomial-time approximation schemes (PTAS) for solving specific constraint satisfaction problems, such as Maximum Independent Set or Minimum Vertex Cover on graph classes that have limited connectivity.

A previously developed approach by Baker achieved PTAS on various graph classes including planar graphs. Further, Romero, Wrochna, and Zivny developed a simpler PTAS for certain graph classes using the Sherali-Adams LP relaxation for maximum CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary non-negative functions.

This research considers CSPs with constraints defined by arbitrary total functions and develops a simpler PTAS across several graph classes using a refined LP relaxation under specific conditions. The results broadens the applicability of PTAS to sparse instances of general-valued CSPs. The research also introduces a new PTAS for Minimum Vertex Cover using a contrasting LP relaxation, extending previous work on maximum CSPs with constraints defined by non-negative functions. The results are obtained without relying on the LP relaxation in question, thereby making the PTAS deterministic. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints on this star's structure and properties, incorporating revised elements such as its chemical composition, surface temperature, and radius. Both scenarios failed to fully account for the observed internal rotation profile, leading to the conclusion that further observations of other stars with similar properties are required to test the theoretical aspects underlying these scenarios. In algorithmic literature, the underlying computation model is typically implicit and assumed to be based on the RAM model. Despite this common assumption, there is a lack of a clear and simple definition of the RAM model. This study seeks to address this ambiguity by providing a precise bounded-alternation RAM (bab RAM) computation model, which is equivalent to the standard RAM model. We demonstrate that in the bab RAM model with only two data storage locations, all arithmetic operations can be performed in a constant time if the base operation is addition, specifically by incorporating a limited form of conditional operation without increasing the constant time complexity. This finding also holds true for the semibab RAM model as well. We show that in the standard RAM model, all arithmetic operations can be performed in a constant time if the base operation is addition, although this requires a deeper algebraic analysis. This study offers a simple and effective definition of the RAM model, which we hope will be useful in the algorithmic community. Additionally, this study provides a memory-bounded ramification of the Sipser-Ladner-Verdier theorem for the bab RAM model. This investigation into the RAM model's properties could lead to interesting outcomes and help broaden the understanding of this fundamental computation model. We examine differential forms on an algebraic compactification of the metric graph moduli space, derived by mapping invariant differential forms from the tropical Torelli map. It's known that these invariant forms give rise to the stable real cohomology of the general linear group, a finding by Borel. We compute period integrals by integrating such forms across graph metrics and find them to be always finite and expressible as generalised Feynman integrals. In various object categorization tasks, particularly in visually complex conditions, it has been demonstrated that recurrent neural networks (RNNs) can outperform feedforward models.  This research aimed to uncover the specific role of RNN recurrence in aiding object categorization.  We trained RNNs on an object categorization task and discovered through linear diagnostic analysis that auxiliary variables such as object position, orientation, and size are communicated through recurrence and contribute significantly to performance improvement.  This evidence confirms our hypothesis that auxiliary variables are utilized to optimize object categorization in cluttered environments.  Notably, while auxiliary variables were found to facilitate recurrence, they were not necessary for learning as exemplified by the emergence of meaningful object features in the input-layer weights of the RNN.  This suggests that auxiliary variables and meaningful object features serve distinct purposes in object categorization.  This study provides the first systematic explanation for the utility of RNN recurrence in object categorization.  Further investigation is needed to establish whether the dependent emergence of these skills has widespread applications across other tasks.  Additionally, the findings highlight the potential for current state-of-the-art object categorization models (big-TNNs) that excel in cluttered environments to benefit from recurrence, implying a competitive edge in performance.  This study offers a novel perspective on object categorization and presents novel findings that can be built upon by the scientific community to advance object categorization methods.  The code for this research can be accessed at https://github.com/keunhan/orthogonality_in_RNNs.  This study was funded by the ANR-17-IDEX-0001 and NSF GRFP programs. Quantum tunneling is an inherent process that lacks a direct analogy in classical physics, and it can rival Coulomb interactions to give rise to intricate phenomena.
In silicon, precise placement of phosphorus dopants is feasible to address the diverse consequences of this interplay, however this approach depends on wave functions related to crystal symmetry, which quantum tunneling inherently affects.
In this study, lattice-precision placement of a single phosphorus atom within a silicon crystal valley enables the separation of spin exchange and Coulomb interactions through analysis of valley coupling patterns.
Valley interference is demonstrated to control the exchange interaction, resulting in a switch between weak and strong coupling by adjusting the valley phase, this discovery opens up opportunities for utilizing a single electron valley degree of freedom for technological applications. Additionally, this research provides insight into the nature of tunneling-based interactions in solids, revealing them to be inherently entangled with Coulomb interactions. Finally, this study unlocks possibilities for realizing a quantum Floquet topological system using a single electron with the aid of silicon's band structure. 
In this work, a new mechanism for controlling interaction in solids is proposed and demonstrated, paving the way for utilizing a single electron valley degree of freedom in technological applications. In cases where Aut(X) is m-transitive for any positive value of m, we define the transitivity degree to be infinite. This study involves determining the transitivity degree for specific varieties, such as quasi-affine toric varieties, and homogeneous spaces, while exploring related open problems. Notably, we avoid reliance on choice or quotient inductive-inductive types, unlike other approaches to dealing with partiality. Designing effective collision avoidance systems for mobile robots remains a key challenge, particularly when accounting for the robot's spatial structure.
In this paper, we develop a novel control approach that leverages Control Barrier Functions and Quadratic Programming to enable safe navigation for mobile robotic arms around obstacles, factoring in their unique geometry.
Our proposed method successfully incorporates geometric constraints by converting them into control constraints, allowing for seamless integration with the robot's spatial structure.
Simulation results for both a simple rod and a modeled robotic arm validate the method's efficiency and scalability, demonstrating its ability to adapt to varying levels of complexity without excessive computation time. Additionally, we explore the integration of this controller with a Kinematic Controller and a Voronoi controller, highlighting potential combinations for practical implementation. Our findings indicate that this controller can provide reliable computation times, even for intricate shapes like a wing, and we observe near-optimal performance in terms of distance and time. In this study, we develop a novel, transcendental interpolation function derived from the hyperbolic tangent, providing more precise approximations of functions that increase linearly with the distance. Building on the Wu-Schaback quasi-interpolation formula, we adapt this new interpolation function while preserving the original scheme's characteristics, including monotonicity and convexity. It has been mathematically proven that our adaptation converges at a rate of O(h^2), enabling smoother interpolation results. Several numerical experiments are presented to demonstrate the method's efficiency and accuracy. Furthermore, we successfully apply the operator to solve free boundary problems. The study demonstrates that the new interpolation function offers improved accuracy compared to previous methods. The gain in convergence rate is particularly pronounced in situations where high precision is required. Pulsar halos are large-scale, high-energy emission structures, formed when energetic electrons and positrons break free from pulsar wind nebulae. As a novel category of gamma-ray emitters, pulsar halos serve as optimal probes for examining the diffusion of cosmic rays within the Galaxy's localized areas, as well as their escape from pulsar wind nebulae. Research on pulsar halos has brought to light that their associated diffusion coefficient is substantially lower than the overall average in the Galaxy, thus building a solid foundation for identifying more concealed pulsar halos and deepening our comprehension of pulsar wind nebulae and radiation. This article delves into the theoretical background and observational evidence for pulsar halos, with a focus on recent findings from the Lambda-CDM model, Langford's model, and a statistical analysis of a sample consisting of 32 pulsar halos identified via the Fermi Lambda Sky Project. It was discovered that pulsar halos account for approximately 7% of the total pulsar population in the Galaxy and that their associated diffusion coefficient is roughly 10 times lower than the overall average. Furthermore, a significant inverse correlation was identified between the pulse period and the halo radius, along with two distinct groups of pulsar halos classified by their location, spatial extension, and diffusion characteristics. The analysis concludes that a classification system consisting of three categories - loose, medium, and tight - accurately describes pulsar halos based on their characteristics and can be utilized for predicting the classification of unseen pulsar halos. Finally, the article discusses the potential for the Fermi All-Sky Survey to contribute to a comprehensive understanding of the Galaxy's diffusion properties through the detection of a substantial number of concealed pulsar halos. Based on the findings, it is anticipated that approximately 50% of all pulsar halos are expected to exhibit a 'loose' type, while a 'tight' type is expected to account for less than 7% of all pulsar halos. The Fermi All-Sky survey is also expected to reveal a direct correlation between the pulsar halo's radius and its associated diffusion coefficient. The research discussed in this article has laid the groundwork for a substantial advancement in our understanding of high-energy radiation emitted by pulsar wind nebulae and the diffusion of cosmic rays in the Galaxy. Additionally, it has provided theoretical backing for a multitude of spectral models, thus building a solid foundation for identifying concealed pulsar halos and deepening our comprehension of the Galaxy's localized diffusion properties

Transportation systems are frequently hindered by unpredictable weather conditions.
Current methods of weather prediction, using either a network of sensors or a vehicle-mounted camera, are limited in scope and costly.
A robust weather detection system is crucial for seamless operation of transportation services in diverse weather conditions.
However, this task is complex due to the varied nature of weather and the scarcity of distinct characteristics that distinguish different weather conditions.
As a result, there is a need for a reliable weather classification system across multiple categories.
Although Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) have been successful in other image recognition tasks, they have yet to be applied to the challenging task of multi-class weather classification. 
Our study introduces a new large-scale weather dataset with 24 classes and examines the performance of pre-trained CNN models, including ResNet-50, on this dataset. 
Our experiments involve evaluating the impact of data augmentation, network fine-tuning, and transfer learning on the accuracy of weather classification. 
Our analysis also compares the performance of CNN models with other pre-trained models, incorporating human annotation of labels to maximize accuracy. 
Our analysis further investigates the effectiveness of CNN models incorporating human annotation of labels to maximize accuracy. 
Our code and dataset are open-source and available for download. 
Our results demonstrate that a modified ResNet-50 architecture, combined with data augmentation and fine-tuning, achieves an impressive top-1 accuracy of 93.74% using camera-mounted data to classify weather conditions. 
Our study represents the first attempt at using CNN models to detect weather conditions from images and lays the groundwork for the development of more accurate deep learning-based weather classification systems in the future. 
Our work has potential applications in various fields, including robotics, vehicle navigation, and aerial imagery.

Our analysis examines how climate change interest shifts among diverse groups and how their individual interests interconnect. Initially, we track the individual trends, followed by developing a cross-influence model that we then validate using a VAR model. Our results indicate significant fluctuations in the general public's climate change interest, as evident from our creation of a Climate Change Index for Europe and the US based on media mentions, whereas economists show relatively little interest as measured by prominent journal publications. Interestingly, science journals and policymakers display a more stable interest in the subject, albeit with policymakers typically becoming interested somewhat later. Notably, there's a noticeable difference in the peaks of interest among various groups, with scientists tending to be more engaged than policymakers, despite the latter group typically becoming interested after the former. This temporal disparity raises important implications, suggesting that scientists may play a crucial role in promoting policy changes. Soft grippers are increasingly popular across various applications due to their versatility and flexibility, yet accurately modeling and controlling them to grasp objects efficiently remains challenging. Soft grippers' infinite-dimensionality and non-linearity make traditional control approaches difficult to implement. In response, researchers have turned to data-driven methods. However, existing methods typically require extensive model learning through simulations or offline processes, which often fails to adapt to novel scenarios or real-time physical robot control requirements. In this research, a novel infinite-dimensional Extended Dynamic Mode Decomposition is proposed, based on the Koopman operator theory, which enables online modeling of soft grippers using real-world data. The model can be utilized to develop predictive models, optimize controllers, and leverage model predictive control to guide soft grippers in real-time. Through simulations and experiments on a multi-fingered soft gripper, it's demonstrated that the proposed method enables online adaptation to diverse objects and environments, even when the model is initialized with incomplete information. Moreover, it outperforms existing methods in grasping performance. The research showcases the potential of using the Koopman operator theory for efficient online control of complex soft robotic systems. The findings may also be extended to other under-actuated and infinite-dimensional systems. The study's code and data are publicly available for verification and future developments. One of the fundamental problems in science and engineering involves finding the lowest cost value for a given function, known as an optimization problem. Various numerical methods have been proposed to solve this problem, but the Gradient Descent method remains the most popular due to its ease and effectiveness. Nonetheless, this approach faces challenges with local minima and slow convergence, particularly when near the optimal point. In response, researchers developed the Natural Gradient Descent method to improve performance across multiple domains, including machine learning, tensor networks, and quantum algorithms. Our work presents a new method to further expand upon NGD, utilizing a suitable reference manifold to expedite convergence and enhance understanding of optimization methods. We demonstrate the success of this approach through applications to neural networks and matrix factorization, outperforming NGD in both scenarios. Additionally, our approach reveals the underlying geometry of these functions, providing new insights into optimization methods. We employed graph invariants, specifically the Jones polynomial, to define the Euclidean metric on the manifold and ensured a smooth, connected structure through the Guillou-Glauber transformation. High-energy emissions from ancient supermassive black holes can provide a direct look into the black hole activity in the early universe. Specifically, misaligned jets of high-redshift active galaxies should make up a significant portion of these distant galaxy populations. This study uses a highly detailed analysis of data collected from multiple observations of a particularly old and distant galaxy called J2102+6015. High-resolution imaging of J2102+6015's energy emissions, which were captured through a highly precise technique called VLBI at a wavelength of 8.4 GHz, revealed two energy-producing regions located about 70 million light-years apart. This imaging was supported by a highly detailed simulation of how J2102+6015's energy emissions behave. It was discovered that one of these regions has the characteristics of being the original energy-producing region at the center of J2102+6015, displaying signs of an original and widespread energy emission pattern often seen in ancient galaxies of this type. In contrast, the other region is thought to be the result of jet activity that is not aligned with other energy-producing regions, which is a common occurrence in galaxies of this type. J2102+6015's energy emissions also showed the presence of molecular gas, which is a key ingredient for the formation of a smooth and unidirectional energy emission pattern in ancient galaxies of this type. Two separate analyses of data collected from observations of J2102+6015 at wavelengths of 8.0 GHz and 8.4 GHz revealed a age of about 0.26 and 0.325 billion years, respectively. These ages are consistent with the likelihood that J2102+6015 is an unaligned jet galaxy, which is a high-energy emission type thought to make up a significant portion of distant galaxy populations. Additionally, J2102+6015's energy emissions also showed the presence of an older and more widespread energy emission pattern often seen in ancient galaxies of this type. This research focuses on improving survival time prediction for lung cancer patients, which, despite significant progress in recent years, still lacks effective methods. Current models, both traditional and deep learning-based, primarily rely on single-textual sources such as patient demographics and clinical history. Unlike existing approaches, this study explores the potential of combining multiple data types like text-based clinical information and visual medical scans to enhance survival time prediction, simulating the decision-making process of a medical professional. Building on this insight, this work introduces the Lite-ProSENet model, which integrates multiple data modalities and significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models, yielding an unprecedented 89.3% concordance in predicting two-year survival probabilities for a specific lung cancer subtype. Moreover, this model and associated method exhibit exceptional generalizability, extending their utility to datasets without and with image data, respectively. Experimental findings, including those applied to datasets without medical scans, demonstrate the validity of the proposed approach. Finally, integration of visual data is found to contribute substantially to survival time prediction, underscoring the importance of utilizing multiple data modalities in complex conditions like lung cancer. The model and associated code have been made publicly available.
