This paper explores the recovery of one-dimensional Radon measures on a torus from their low-frequency Fourier components up to a given cutoff frequency, denoted as Kc. The proposed method involves minimizing the total variation among all compatible Radon measures through the problem of basis pursuit in the continuum (BPC). We demonstrate that a unique solution exists and is equally spaced with respect to the Fourier frequencies in the range of -Kc to Kc. Additionally, the paper discusses two distinct algorithms for solving BPC: a real-valued variant of the Chord Method and a complex-valued algorithm based on Newton iterations. Notably, the number of iterations required for both methods is directly proportional to the total number of discrete points in the range of -Kc to Kc. Furthermore, the paper introduces a novel scheme, known as complex aggregation, which allows for a significant reduction in computational requirements by taking advantage of the inherent structure in the problem, particularly when the range of -Kc to Kc contains a large number of discrete points. In such scenarios, the method necessitates only a proportionally smaller number of iterations, thereby improving its computational efficiency. The theoretical findings presented here are accompanied by corresponding numerical experiments, which demonstrate that the proposed methods can effectively recover low-frequency components in various challenging scenarios, including synthetic and real-world data sets, thereby setting a benchmark for reference. The paper culminates by highlighting the diverse range of applications where recovering low-frequency components has pivotal implications. These areas of study encompass research domains such as geophysical inversion, magnetic resonance imaging, and data compression, thus underscoring the broad potential impact of the underlying problem and the proposed solutions. P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for syntax analysis and translation of P416 programs into hardware-independent code, but a compiler backend to map this code to V1Model switch resources is needed. A freely available compiler backend for P416 programs and V1Model architecture-based switches has been missing until now. Commercial solutions exist but come with restrictive terms, hindering research into mapping P416 programs onto programmable switches. Our work fills this gap with an open-source compiler backend for the V1Model architecture, utilizing heuristic optimization to improve resource usage on the switch. This allows direct comparison with other approaches and provides alternatives to vendor-specific solutions, according to our evaluation. The compiler backend, along with our source code, is publicly accessible. Future research can build upon our foundation by exploring novel mapping strategies. Additionally, we found that further optimizations are possible, particularly when targeting specific applications, which we illustrated by improving the resource usage on a switch when mapping a P416 program derived from an SDN architecture. Moreover, we found that resource usage could be improved when the mapping of P416 programs to switch resources is left flexible during configuration. In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas elements are widely used to approximate vector-valued variables like velocity or momentum. Nevertheless, the standard finite element methods that employ the lowest-order quadrilateral Raviart-Thomas elements tend to have low spatial accuracy in the vector transport equation. This paper explores two methods that elevate the accuracy of transporting such vector-valued fields across curved surfaces in two-dimensional environments. One method builds upon existing notions of transport operators with added components; the other draws upon projective constraints to project the field normal to the transport direction. These methods' performance will be tested with a variety of rotating and curved fluid flows. Ultimately, our research aims to provide high-accuracy numerical tools for simulating curved fluid motions. Details about extending our methods to three-dimensional scenarios can be found in a corresponding arXiv paper (arXiv:2106.11379). It includes simulations of three-dimensional rotating curved flows. Furthermore, our research delves into the theoretical underpinnings of these methods, addressing questions of existence, uniqueness, and stability in related continuous models. This analysis sheds light on the design of numerical schemes and informs their design. In the last few years, the creation of accurate numerical solutions for problems with Hamiltonian dynamics led to the establishment of a specific class of energy-preserving Runge-Kutta methods known as Hamiltonian Boundary Value Methods (HBVMs). These methods can be interpreted as a continuous, multi-step approach, similar to Runge-Kutta methods but with continuous stages, and are explored here in the context of more general differential problems. This leads to the development of a broader class of energy-preserving methods, known as Hamiltonian Continous Stage Methods (HCSMs), which maintain the previous efficient properties while being adaptable for a wider range of problems. HCSMs are further analyzed and efficiently implemented to solve different second and third order ODE problems, and their performance is compared with other prevailing numerical methods. This includes a thorough investigation of their order of convergence and their ability to preserve energy in non-conservative systems, demonstrating significant advantages. Ultimately, HCSMs provide an innovative, flexible option for numerically solving a variety of problems, particularly those with underlying dynamic structures, and could be extended to accommodate a more general understanding of differential problems in the future. This paper introduces an innovative approach called local critic training, a model-parallel learning method utilizing specialized networks to refine neural network updates. By segmenting the main network into separate layer groups and applying error gradients from corresponding critic modules to these segments, the learning process is efficiently decoupled. As a result, the update process can be completed in a much smaller batch size for each iteration. Interestingly, this update process still converges to an optimal equilibrium despite the smaller batch size. Building on this concept, multiple critics are trained in parallel to accelerate the learning process further. Empirical evidence demonstrates that local critic training yields significant speedups in model-parallel learning experiments across various network structures and datasets. Moreover, it offers a reliable solution to the issue of communication overhead in distributed training. Notably, local critic training has successfully implemented end-to-end federated learning in mobile networks, achieving speedup in training time. The code for local critic training is publicly available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/jaejunslee/local-critic-training. A demonstration of local critic training can be found here: https://github.com/jaejunslee/local-critic-training/blob/main/local_critic_training_demo.ipynb. This research was funded by the NSF grant #2047592 and #2146912. We would like to express our gratitude to Wei Deng, Jialin Ye, and Jia Liu for their valuable contributions to this research. Finally, local critic training offers a versatile approach to model-parallel learning that can be adaptable to a broad range of applications, including but not limited to neural architecture search, transfer learning, and multi-task learning. Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart. In this research, a three-dimensional open Hamiltonian system is analyzed where the non-dissipative boundaries initially deviate from Wada's characteristics, changing topologically. Focusing on the effects of dissipation, this study investigates how this system alters when weak dissipation lowers the system's energy below its critical value. Interestingly, this investigation finds that non-dissipative Wada basins transform into semi-Wada basins and ultimately hybrid basins as weak dissipation decreases the critical energy. Semi-Wada basins exhibit an intermediate topological structure, combining both Wada and hybrid basin properties. Prior studies have only found hybrid basins in non-dissipative systems. This study contradicts previous predictions that Wada basins cannot survive weak dissipation. Instead, it demonstrates that Wada basins can persist in the form of semi-Wada basins under such conditions. Furthermore, this research analyses the interplay between escape rates and dissipation strengths, establishing a new relation that holds across all stages, from non-dissipative systems to those beyond critical dissipation. Ultimately, this research distinguishes between two different scenarios for system behavior beyond critical dissipation, each characterized by different escape rate patterns driven by distinct system dynamics. Lastly, this study highlights the potential of using escape rates to distinguish between different phases of dissipative systems. It also emphasizes the importance of employing a multi-scale analysis in such systems to avoid drawing incorrect conclusions based on local observations. Finally, various routes to chaos have multiple physical interpretations and multiple causes, and this study provides quantitative analyses that match qualitatively with the different routes to chaos. Lastly, key indicators of different chaotic behaviors, such as correlations, entropies, and fractals, are provided. They serve as reference points for distinguishing between different phases of chaotic systems and provide a basis for comparing other three-dimensional open Hamiltonian systems with those studied here. They also provide a basis for comparing these systems with other two-dimensional chaotic systems. It is hypothesized that a comprehensive phase diagram, illustrating the relationships between different phases of chaotic systems, could be developed using these indicators. This article will examine the concept of star formation (SF) through observation, and its progression over time, offering a fresh understanding of the process, particularly relevant since planet formation emerges from it and sheds new light on the origins of life in the universe. We intend to provide an in-depth explanation of the observed phenomena of SF, focusing on its initial stages, to ultimately derive the fundamental conditions necessary for its occurrence. 

I. Introduction to Star Formation Observations
The study of SF aims to reveal the underlying mechanisms of this essential cosmic event. To accomplish this, researchers have relied heavily on the latest in observational technology. This article will provide an overview of the key findings and the methodology employed in the field of SF observations.

II. Protostellar Candidates Selection
The identification of young stars is crucial in understanding the SF process. We discuss the criteria for distinguishing protostars from other celestial objects and the established classification system for young stars.

III. The Observed Properties of Young Stars
This section delves into the characteristics of young stars previously undetectable using other methods, focusing on their formation environment, structure, and motion. Specifically, we examine the moving groups of young stars and their dispersion.

IV. The Conditions for Star Formation
By analyzing the data on the formation of stars, researchers have learned that these events occur under specific conditions, particularly in relation to the magnetic field in molecular clouds. This study demonstrates the existence of feeble, measure-valued solutions to a first-order nonlinear hyperbolic conservation law under fairly minimal prerequisites for a large class of initial conditions. In particular, quite relaxed conditions are imposed on the nonlinear flux function. A suitable solution is defined as one that satisfies a related equation in the weak sense within the domain and is consistent with the initial condition. An efficient tool employed in the proof is a specific version of Breschard's theorem, which is itself a key finding of this investigation. It has important implications for similar equations, such as those involving nonlinear Schrödinger equations and certain multicomponent systems. Interestingly, quite minimal conditions are imposed on the nonlinear flux function. An important observation is that solutions may take the form of a sum of two continuous functions, one of which is increasing everywhere and represents the cumulative distribution function of a non-increasing measure. In particular, this result applies to equations where the nonlinear flux function increases at a polynomial rate. In contrast, it was previously proven that solutions exist and are continuous when the flux function increases at an exponential rate. Furthermore, it was proven that solutions are unique and have a specific oscillation restriction when the flux function increases at a power greater than half. We have developed a numerical approach to maximize coupling efficiency in single-photon sources consisting of a quantum dot-cavity and a ridge waveguide by conducting simulations using the finite element method. A design optimized for a 1D nanobeam cavity yielded a notable source efficiency of 97.7 percent and an impressive Purcell factor of 38.6 for an isotropic dipole, primarily due to a combination of high index contrast between GaAs and SiO$_2$ materials and an effective cavity design that facilitated interference and minimized losses. However, we also identified mode mismatch as a limitation of our platform and devised an optimization technique to achieve high efficiency in single-photon sources. This method incorporates a taper section to smoothly bridge the mode mismatch between the quantum dot-cavity and the ridge waveguide. As a result, the optimized nanocavity source achieved an exceptional efficiency of nearly 99 percent and a substantial Purcell factor of around 50. Furthermore, we examined the effects of feature size variations on the system and applied our techniques to improve a 2D photonic crystal cavity-based single-photon source, ultimately enhancing its efficiency by about 60 percent. Additionally, we observed that incorporating a taper in the system reduced antibunching visibility losses but had minimal impact on its spectral properties. Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool that not only allows for the identification of a glass's vibrational modes near its boson peak, but also provides insight into the specific motions involved, thereby facilitating the calculation of dynamic structure factor and sound wave proportions within and below the boson peak frequency. Research on numerous glasses has revealed that the boson peak's characteristics can be effectively described by a power-law dependence on the density of glassy systems, and has also accessed information on glassy dynamics through measurements of dynamic autocorrelation functions over very long time scales, using the time-of-flight neutron spectrometer NOM. This instrument's unique capabilities have further enabled researchers to investigate the role of quasifree vibrations in the dynamics of supercooled liquids and glasses, an area in which significant knowledge gaps existed. Overall, the application of neutron inelastic scattering has significantly advanced understanding of glassy dynamics. Its potential for generating new hypotheses and questions should continue to drive experimental work, combining with molecular dynamics simulations to test these hypotheses, to further explore the unique dynamics of amorphous materials. This review also highlights areas for further investigation. The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings is that they must remain stable - preventing the situation where two agents would prefer each other over their respective matches. Variants of the Stable Roommates problem, including those involving larger groups of agents and distinct valuation methods, offer alternative scenarios for exploring agent matchings. A more complex form of the Stable Roommates problem, incorporating additively separable valuations and three-dimensional groupings, was explored, revealing instances where no stable matches exist and a direct approach is NP-complete, even when using limited binary valuations. However, under the condition of binary and symmetric valuations, we found that a stable matching will always exist and can be found within polynomial time. Large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computing relies heavily on topological error correction codes like the surface code, underscoring the need for efficient and adaptable decoding methods, especially in the presence of faulty measurements. This study transforms the full fault-tolerant decoding problem into a learning process involving a decoder interacting with a code environment, to which reinforcement learning principles can be applied to develop effective decoding tools. Using deepQ learning as an example, we successfully created rapid surface code decoders capable of handling multiple types of noise models. Deep reinforcement learning allowed us to create robust decoders in as little as 15 minutes on a standard GPU, far outperforming previous studies. Furthermore, we discovered that deep reinforcement learning decoders continue to function at high speeds without the need for further optimization, an advantage when compared to traditional decoder techniques, which often reach performance plateaus at low error rates. Finally, we investigate the effects of limited training data on these decoders and explore the potential integration of feedback loops for enhanced performance in realistic quantum computing scenarios. This study lays the foundation for the development of efficient decoder tools, an essential step towards achieving fault-tolerant quantum computing. The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased yields, exceeding $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This excess, observed at large angles and low hadron $p_T$, is more pronounced for hadrons linked to lower-momentum direct photons, indicating an increased response of the medium to deposited energy. Au$+$Au collisions exhibit direct photon yields equivalent to $p$$+$$p$ collisions, suggesting a complete hadronization of heavy ions. Observations of hadrons linked to high-momentum direct photons are less modified in their momentum distribution compared to hadrons created in association with lower-momentum direct photons. This contrast implies the medium responds differently to high-energy deposits, influenced by the inherent jet characteristics and complex interactions with the surrounding medium. Scattering mechanisms pose significant challenges to traditional optical control systems, rendering them infeasible for practical use in tissues. In this research, a novel approach combining a binary-level iterative learning algorithm with a digital phase mask is introduced, leveraging its inherent robustness to phase noise to effectively control wave dynamics through turbulent media. Numerical simulations reveal its capability to form multiple complex structures within a 3D volume despite the presence of strong scattering, outperforming existing methods by up to 90% in terms of control error. Furthermore, this system's versatility has been demonstrated through its successful application to forming an optical axis and achieving high light concentration within a 3D tissue-like medium. Simulation results reveal an impressive 99.5% convergence rate, 97.5% photon utilization, and less than 2% control error. Specifically, this research holds the promise of enabling immunotherapy targeting, precise single-cell activation, and the deployment of portable, hand-held light sources for medical treatments and imaging. Meta-analyses that include multiple trials based on shared study participants often report correlated effect sizes.  In these situations, employing cluster-robust variance estimators can effectively synthesize dependent effects, however they may produce inflated Type 1 errors in cases of a limited number of studies.  Two new cluster-robust estimators have been developed for bivariate meta-regression models utilizing a simulated dataset based on 1000 replicates.  These estimators outperformed traditional methods in assessing publication bias, demonstrating improved performance in model estimation and hypothesis testing, particularly when dealing with small sample sizes.  Notably, one of the proposed estimators exhibited improved performance in both efficiency and robustness.  These findings suggest that both estimators are viable alternatives to established methods in bivariate meta-regression analyses, particularly when working with non-normal data and the presence of small sample sizes.  Software code for replicating the results is available upon request to the corresponding author.  Two new estimators have been suggested for future research: (i) an extension of the Petersen et al. (2012) estimator for dealing with correlated effect sizes in mixed-effects meta-regression; (ii) an adaptation of the cluster-robust estimator (McCullough & Sulieman, 2006) in the context of bivariate meta-regression models.  The latter may offer improved performance when data is normally distributed and sample sizes are sufficiently large.  These estimators have been tested in a range of scenarios, and their potential areas of application include analyzing within-study correlations and incorporating covariates in a synthesis.  Future work can build upon these ideas by exploring additional areas of computation.  In contrast, the influence of study size on test results can be addressed through alternative approaches.  A key discovery of our research was the finite sample performance of the model-based estimator in the context of bivariate meta-regression models, and the potential benefits of incorporating it into future analyses.  Two new ideas have been suggested for future research: (i) an extension of the concept of influence to bivariate meta-regression contexts; (ii) a general approach for simulating data based on a given statistical model.  Additionally, our research has directly addressed a previously unanswered query regarding the efficacy of the model-based estimator in small sample sizes.  A key contribution of our research is the development of a framework for estimating influence measures in the context of bivariate meta-regression models, and the demonstration of its practical utility through code available upon request. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive. As such, this method aims to enable larger time steps for particle collisions while maintaining accurate simulation results. Essential collision rules have been modified to make them independent of time steps, allowing for the use of larger time steps in simulations. Multiple time steps can be employed to integrate fluid and particle motions separately. To test its effectiveness, this method has been applied to collision simulations involving elastic and plastic particles, demonstrating improved stability and accuracy. Furthermore, this algorithm has been used to simulate complex particle collisions in diverse conditions, demonstrating its ability to accurately model particle collisions at larger time steps. Additionally, this method has been validated against existing models showing equivalent results. This method has the potential to greatly simplify particle-resolved simulations by enabling larger time steps, enhancing its overall efficiency. This simulation code is publicly available at github.com/epfl-pcpi/particles-for-cfd. This study was financially supported by EPFL's Blue Sky Research fund. S.G. acknowledges the support from Fonds de la Recherche Scientifique (FRS-FNRS) through an Postdoctoral Mobility Scholarship. This work was performed using open-source software such as Palabos, OpenFOAM, and Python with numerical libraries NumPy, Matplotlib and Scipy. Specifically, Palabos version 5.0 had to be modified significantly to implement the multi-time-step integration method described in this study. This modification is now available in the development branch dev-5-x-specialized-particle-collision-algorithms of the Palabos public GitHub repository. High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve this, as data in such memory types can remain accessible during power outages. Nevertheless, the high failure rates of server-class processors and other components in modern systems still necessitate efficient crash recovery mechanisms. Given the non-volatile memory's capabilities, researchers have focused less on traditional rollback recovery and instead explored new approaches. This paper evaluates the efficacy of algorithm-based crash recovery, specifically for sort operations, as an example of data processing, highlighting the potential benefits and limitations of this technique for high-performance computing applications. Evaluation using the HPC scaling simulator revealed that the baseline algorithm reaches near crash-recovery speeds on 40 servers, with the potential for further optimization when combining this technique with other fault-tolerance methods. Furthermore, results from running sort on the Minerva cluster showed that including check operations significantly increases the time and energy costs, underscoring the need to carefully evaluate the trade-offs in any algorithm-based crash-recovery solution. These findings imply that implementing a straightforward base algorithm on top of non-volatile memory can be a viable means of achieving crash recovery in HPC systems. Moving forward, researchers can build upon this foundation, aiming to develop efficient fault-tolerant algorithms capable of efficiently processing data across large-scale HPC systems. At the same time, there is a need for more comprehensive fault-tolerance testing on existing high-performance computing systems, including the national and international clusters like (e.g. Tres-2, Sierra, Summit), to validate the efficacy of this technique in real-world applications. Additionally, it is anticipated that algorithm-based crash recovery will also have practical uses in other areas, such as database management. To explore this possibility, we have also carried out a small-scale evaluation (using the testing framework from the Netflix Stadium, comprising 96 Cores and 192 GB RAM) focused on checking the potential for crash-recovery in the sorting algorithm "ints-sort". While we did not expect this to be feasible, our results showed that including check operations in this algorithm leads to a considerable slowdown, suggesting that any future implementations aiming to combine fault-tolerance means with algorithm-based crash recovery will need to carefully evaluate the trade-offs in such approaches. Consequently, it remains to be seen whether it will be feasible to efficiently combine (as an example) memory replication and rollback with roll-forward techniques in order to achieve reliable fault-tolerant high-performance computing operations. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. The evaluation shows HDTM outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy and scalability. The implemented model is further demonstrated in an online application available at hierarchical.io. The application allows users to navigate a searchable hierarchy within Wikipedia and reveals its underlying structure as a hierarchy graph. The generated hierarchy is computed in real-time using HDTM and is adaptable to various datasets, encompassing domains such as digital libraries, semantic web, and online documentation. The hierarchical structure is presently displayed on Wikipedia under the heading of Hierarchical Organization. The implementation details of this application, including the hierarchy computation, are detailed in a companion article on Wikipedia's API. The code for this research is openly available on GitHub at https://github.com/hierarchical/io. The model's focus on preserving the inherent interconnections in modern information networks results in a more authentic and meaningful hierarchical structure. The evaluation shows HDTM's computational efficiency, enabling its application to datasets of various sizes, including Wikipedia's full content. We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding theoretical models. By running and analyzing one million simulations for diverse initial conditions, both with and without equal masses in three-body systems, we were able to achieve precise statistical accuracy. Four distinct measures were used to characterize distribution shapes, including the development of new parameters and skewness indices. This research confirmed the precision of a proposed statistical model, revealing a close alignment between theoretical and simulated results for most parameters. Notably, our findings also highlight variations between certain theoretical and simulated values, particularly for certain kurtosis measures. This disparity prompts further investigation into underlying causes. Additionally, our studies validate a previously postulated hypothesis concerning distribution forms, while also exploring corresponding physical implications. Based on these outcomes, we suggest both statistical and physical reasons underlying the predicted statistical shapes in three-body systems. These reasons may ultimately inform future clinical trials in astrophysical contexts. Finally, our research lays out a statistical framework that can be employed to assess and validate numerical integrations in three-body systems, highlighting potential sources of error inherent to such methods. This research is expected to contribute to numerical integrations in astrophysical simulations, particularly regarding binary interactions and the diffusion of their parameters. Finally, our studies provide fresh perspectives on the long-standing (homogeneous) three-body problem. To better reflect this, we propose the term "Flux Paradox," representing a puzzle that has persisted for centuries in the realm of classical physics. This research is meant to inspire relevant studies in astrophysics, utilizing numerical data to shed light on the predictions of various statistical models. Furthermore, our outcome is anticipated to be extendable to higher-dimensional systems, with potential applications including clotting phenomena and microbial swarming. On a broader note, our work demonstrates the utility of numerical astrophysics in investigating and validating theoretical predictions, thus highlighting the mutual beneficial aspects of both disciplines. This research was made possible through a collaborative combination of numerical astrophysics and theoretical physics approaches. To facilitate this, we incorporated and adapted modern software tools, including Python, in an original manner. This, in turn, prompted the development of original resources, including tutorials, that may be accessed through dedicated repositories for educational purposes. This way, our studies continue to contribute to the broader ecosystem of classical physics, even as we build towards a related project centered on numerical astrophysics. Erdos originally proposed a conjecture suggesting that $a_n > c \cdot 2^n$, with the current record at $a_n > c \cdot 2^n/\sqrt{n}$. This article presents modified constraints where we investigate lower and upper bounds for the minimum possible value of $a_n$. Additionally, this article explores variants involving vectors of integers and other constraints. Imitation learning seeks to bypass the complexity of creating optimal reward functions for agent training by utilizing expert behavior instead.  A common challenge in imitation learning is filtering out irrelevant actions yielded by noisy state observations, which can generate substantial policy distortion. Research has proposed several methods to resolve this issue; however, these approaches often rely on the availability of an expert policy. This paper presents a new model, called domain-guided imitation learning. The proposed method overcomes the challenge mentioned above without relying on an expert policy and generalizes across domains without requiring explicit domain representation. Our model achieves this by utilizing a separate discriminator network to estimate a domain-invariant state distribution. Through this estimation, our model is able to remove spurious correlations present in noisy state observations and increase the imitation ratio significantly. We demonstrate the efficacy of our model through experiments involving robotic manipulation tasks. The proposed model successfully imitates novel tasks and demonstrates generalization capabilities across domains through multiple empirical examples. Furthermore, our model outperforms existing methods in imitation learning by significantly reducing policy distortion and imitating a variety of tasks. We conducted a series of simulations of magnetohydrodynamics, running up to 1000 years following the initial protostar formation. Generating synthetic spoken languages with real speakers is an efficient way to expand spoken language training data for a limited set of speakers. But current approaches that rely on non-realistic synthetic speech are of no use to existing models, and require significant effort to deliver decent results. We've developed an alternative method that uses minimal editing to create natural-sounding speech with human-like effort, and is compatible with leading speech-to-text and translation models. This new method, known as modulated data augmentation, not only produces high-quality synthetic data but also trains models to generalize better across related languages. Our tests using speech-to-text data show that using synthetic data generated with this method yields better recognition accuracy than data augmentation methods that don't use synthetic data, and translation quality also improves when training on synthetic data, especially for low-resource languages. Our code and synthetic datasets are available for public use.

It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis. Additionally, a theoretical investigation on the properties of the estimator is conducted. Achieving dependable data privacy while ensuring data utility is an intricate problem in various real-world applications. To address this issue, a novel framework known as One-Sided Differential Privacy (OSDP) has been developed. OSDP enhances data utility by recognizing that not every data record contains sensitive information. However, the previous approaches in this field made the assumption that data records were statistically independent from one another. Inspired by occupancy patterns in multi-person scenarios such as meetings or transactions, this study examines dependent data sets in a real-world context. The current approach, specifically Adaptive Release based on Logarithmic Perturbation (ALP), may be suitable for a single data relation but fails when dealing with inter-dependent data relationships. Consequently, this study introduces two improved mechanisms: Additive Relation Protection (ARP) and Exponential Relation Protection (ERP). The proposed ERP mechanism is demonstrated to have a better data utility-to-leakage ratio compared to ALP. The study also introduces an evaluation method to assess the risk of privacy breaches (PBL) in dependent data sets. The experimental results confirm that ERP offers superior privacy-quality ratios, reducing privacy breaches while maintaining data utility. In model planet-forming disks like AS 209, deviations from typical radial gas and dust distributions are observed. Notably, CO gas is found to decline dramatically at a specific distance from the star. Two primary theories underpinning this CO drop-off are examined: the idea that it results in reduced CO molecule availability, and the notion that it stems from altered CO molecule formation and destruction rates due to temperature and chemical conditions. To investigate this further, calculations of gas and ice formation are carried out, with and without nitrogen-based chemical radicals, leading to the identification of parameter sets that accurately match observed data. These experiments demonstrate that radial changes in radical abundance can lead to CO depletion, but that certain model settings require the gas radical be carried by particles rather than in a free state, resulting in inadequate depletion. Furthermore, observations of CO symmetry stretching mode in both AS 209 and another object, HD 163307, fail to display evidence of reduced CO molecule coverage, instead indicating it remains largely unchanged at distances from the star where CO depletion is observed. This implies that CO molecule coverage is not solely responsible for gas and dust ring formations in AS 209. While ice formation is found to result in CO molecule coverage levels that almost perfectly match observed data at certain distances from the star, at closer distances to the star, model settings yield coverage levels significantly lower than those observed. In contrast, temperature-driven CO molecule coverage matches observed data at all measured distances. Lastly, the impact of nitromethane, a product of nitrous acid and HCO+, on CO molecule coverage is explored. While it's hypothesized that CO+ recombination could generate nitromethane, it's also suggested that it could simply be an overlooked byproduct of a highly reactive species, one that has a significant effect on CO molecule coverage levels in AS 209. Nonetheless, the hypothesis also suggests that CO+ recombination could itself result in CO molecule coverage levels, but only at closer distances to the star. At a distance just short of 35 AU, both ice formation and temperature-driven CO molecule coverage fail to account for observed CO molecule coverage levels, but it's hypothesized that this could be the result of CO molecule coverage regulated through processes unrelated to planet formation. Ultimately, it's concluded that radial CO molecule depletion in AS 209 is likely the result of multiple factors, but that CO molecule coverage levels are not primarily regulated by CO molecule coverage or CO molecule coverage regulated through planets. Rather, it's hypothesized that CO molecule depletion is primarily the result of highly reactive species

The analysis of time-stamped data is a fundamental aspect of scientific and industrial research, where the vast amount of generated data poses significant processing challenges due to increased resolution, input channels, and event acquisition rates. To overcome these obstacles, we've created the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), an advanced, yet intuitive software solution that streamlines time-stamped data analysis and visualization. Leveraging an integrated approach of flowcharts and modular code snippets, our tool empowers users to perform intricate data correlation and analysis, while maintaining high computational performance and efficiency. ETA features a user-friendly interface, enabling analysts to perform tasks with minimal setup and execution time, and offers a range of pre-defined analysis templates for common applications, including the analysis of Time-of-Flight (TOF) data, and the evaluation of detector performance and event activation patterns. Furthermore, ETA's robust framework and seamless integration with MATLAB/LOS allow for seamless integration with other research tools, making it an ideal solution for scientists and engineers struggling with the analysis of vast amounts of time-stamped data. This paper introduces ETA, a versatile analysis solution, and showcases its capabilities in a real-world application, specifically with detector characterization using ToF data. This outcome builds upon Cannarsa and Capuani's research, adapting it to apply to mean field games of controls with velocities as controls. The existence of an equilibrium in this context is challenged by requiring the necessary regularity of controls, a requirement we overcome by imposing a small Lipschitz constraint on the dependence of the Lagrangian function on the joint measure of states and controls, and showing that under these constraints regular paths can be closely approximated. This allows us to demonstrate the existence of a mean field game with the desired properties, enabling a trajectory that is'mildly consistent'. The proof involves establishing a necessary condition for the equilibrium, demonstrating the existence of a path that is close to average under certain conditions, and showing that this path can be reached by a sequence of controls. The latter step involves assuming the closure of a set of admissible controls and establishing a convenient metric for the purposes of this argument. Recent analyses of Gaia data have led to the discovery of new stellar structures, a newly classified type known as stellar "strings". We conducted an in-depth examination of these structures, focusing on their spatial patterns, movement, chemical composition, and whether their members originated from a shared location. By analyzing the distribution of these structures in 3D space, we discovered that they do not exhibit the bell-shaped pattern typically seen in other clusters. Instead, the distances of their members span a wide range and often contradict earlier estimates of their age and size. Further investigation into the movement of these structures revealed that they do not move as a single unit but rather with varying rates and directions. Multifiber spectroscopy of a stellar string showed that its members have differing chemical compositions, further indicating they did not originate from a single source. These findings suggest that the concept of stellar "strings" may not accurately represent coeval families born from a shared cloud. Rather, they can be viewed as random collections of stars that happen to share similar distances and motions, forming the basis for their classification as associations in Gaia data. By reevaluating the classification of these structures, we can refine our understanding of stellar population analysis and how to effectively utilize Gaia data. Additionally, we propose a new method for reducing systematic errors in distance measurements, providing highly accurate readings for these structures and other star clusters. This technique can also inform our knowledge of various structures across the galaxy's bulge. Finally, we suggest key areas for further study, including high-resolution imaging and rapid follow-up spectroscopy for further disentangling these structures and uncovering their true natures. These efforts could lead to a deeper understanding of the galaxy's complex history and the formation of its various components. To aid in these future studies, we have included detailed maps and lists of these structures, including their members and key data, which can be found on our website. These assets also include a tool for calculating radial velocities and identifying potential targets for further spectroscopic analysis. Additionally, we have included raw and processed data, as well as custom software, that can be used to replicate our analysis and expand on the findings, especially regarding the wide-ranging distances of these structures and the need for further study and observation. This can be found on our website, along with the data and code, under the heading "supplementary materials". We have also included a public version of the website, where users can access this supplementary material, under the following address: https://www.astro-latvia.lv/~z Zipris/index.php

For visually appealing outfits, individual garments must harmoniously fit together based on factors like style, type, and color. Current studies view visual compatibility as a straightforward'match' or'mismatch' classification problem, where each garment item is labeled as entirely compatible or incompatible. Yet, this simplistic approach is impractical for real-world Outfit Maker apps where users must identify which specific items might clash with their created outfits. To address this limitation, we introduce the Visual InCompatibility TransfORmer (VICTOR) that's tailored to tackle two distinct challenges: quantifying an outfit's overall compatibility and pinpointing individual mismatched items. Leveraging a fashion-oriented language-image contrastive pre-training framework, we fine-tune VICTOR on a wide range of fashion visuals. We expand upon the Polyvore outfit benchmark, introducing a dataset dubbed Polyvore-MISFITs comprising imperfectly matched outfits, to train and test our proposed model. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our proposed VICTOR outperforms or matches state-of-the-art performance on the Polyvore dataset while achieving an impressive 88% reduction in computational requirements, striking an ideal balance between accuracy and efficiency. We publicly release the VICTOR implementation at https://github.com/stevejpapad/Visual-InCompatibility-Transformer. Additionally, the demo app built with the VICTOR model is available at https://stevejpapad.github.io/Visual-InCompatibility-Transformer. Simplified web demos of this work can also be found on the Outfit Maker platform and the VICTOR website. This research is an extended version of the paper first presented at the 2022 CVPR conference. We've incorporated numerous feedback from the 2022 CVPR workshop and a nearby Spark AI Research press conference. This research is currently being presented at the 2023 NeurIPS conference under the name 'Outfit Compatibility at your Fingertips,' with a corresponding video available at https://youtu.be/8Rr8R7RJ1kY. A companion highlight box is available on arXiv, with the full paper available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.13552. A floating raft made of particles offers a clear model for observing material breakdown. Due to the slow timescales, both how the particles move back to a more stable configuration and the formation of cracks within the raft can be measured precisely. When we extend a raft made of particles by expanding its surface, we see that its breaking pattern changes constantly based on the rate at which we are stretching it. If we stretch the raft slowly, its edges will move towards the center due to particle interplay, causing it to crack inside. However, if we stretch it quickly, the particles on the new surface will gather at the thinnest point, leading to a more uneven breaking pattern. Our observations using high-speed microscopes have shown that these reactions are not affected by the rate of stretching, regardless of the viscosity of the surrounding fluid. This is different from what happens when a liquid starts breaking up into droplets due to an external force, where a specific point, known as the 'effective viscosity' varies based on the force and the liquid's thickness. Similarly, our research using computer simulations has shown that the timescales at which a raft made of particles breaks up are directly linked to its mechanical properties and not influenced by external factors, unlike systems where a liquid starts breaking up into droplets. This distinction has allowed us to clarify the underlying factors governing a specific type of material breakdown and our research has provided a precise model for understanding this process, which usually occurs quickly and can only be observed for a short period of time. This new model can be applied to other complex materials that are often studied near a point of collapse. By combining traditional and original styles of thinking about material breakdown, we have developed a precise understanding of the basic processes governing a raft made of particles and have presented our research in an easily accessible way. At the same time, our research has shown that a common mathematical tool, known as 'hydrodynamics', can be applied not just to liquids but also to particles in motion, offering a new and unexpected connection between two previously distinct areas of thought. This understanding of particle flow has enabled us to quantify and analyze the underlying factors governing a raft made of particles, where particle behavior is often governed by different rules, including friction and attraction towards each other and external surfaces. By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods. Our results show that SPGP-SARSA surpasses the performance of state-of-the-art TD methods while consuming less computational resources than rejection-based methods.  Our findings also highlight SPGP-SARSA's potential for real-world application by successfully translating to a real-world navigation task. We analyze the statistical approximation of the $L^2$-operator defined as $[Pf](x) = \mathbb{E}[f(Y) | X = x]$ given the joint distribution of $X$ and $Y$ on a certain topological space under minimal assumptions. It is comparable to a parametric operator which involves a infinite-dimensional space of functions. It can be seen as a type of nonparametric posterior in Bayesian inference which has drawn significant attention in theoretical Bayesian statistics in recent years. This note enhances and reinforces Bates' theorem which indicates that for row-finite graphs classified as strong shift equivalent, their associated graph C*-algebras are also Morita equivalent. This discovery opens up possibilities to investigate if the stronger notion of Morita equivalence effectively describes strong shift equivalence. This line of inquiry will likely hold true for graphs exhibiting finite symbolic dynamical systems, yet we contend that Bates' theorem isn't entirely comprehensive by illustrating a counterexample involving two strong shift equivalent graphs whose C*-algebras do not demonstrate Morita equivalence. This counterexample has broader implications, suggesting that the model invariants used to identify graph C*-algebras aren't reliable indicators of strong shift equivalence. Moreover, this analysis extends to identify paths of strong shift equivalent graphs, each with a C*-algebra that is not Morita equivalent to the others. Ultimately, this research poses a key question: are there instances of strong shift equivalent graphs with C*-algebras that are not Morita equivalent? This area of study remains contingent upon resolving a related question posed by the provided counterexample: can the graph embedding model be used to create a row-finite graph exhibiting strong shift equivalence, yet with a C*-algebra that isn't Morita equivalent to all others. If such an instance exists, it would contradict Bates' theorem and suggest that Morita equivalence doesn't comprehensively describe strong shift equivalence. Consequently, this would prompt an examination of a potentially broader equivalence class containing strong shift equivalence, which may include insulator algebras, indicating that this class might not be cohesive under this broader interpretation. As a starting point to address this question, we present a theorem demonstrating that for any insulator algebra, its graph can be transformed into one exhibiting trivial conic structure through a series of row overdrive operations. This fundamental result has far-reaching implications, suggesting that insulator algebras might be equivalently classified with strong shift equivalence by removing these structural modifications. Nonetheless, this transformation analysis gives rise to further generalised concepts, such as (pseudo) insulator algebras and eventually insulator algebras, which may represent a larger equivalence class containing strong shift equivalence, while also potentially encompassing the class of Morita equivalent algebras. This line of inquiry remains contingent upon resolving two key open questions: can any eventually insulator algebra be reinterpreted as a (pseudo) insulator algebra via row overdrive operations and do these alterations eventually eliminate all off-diagonal path projections, thereby achieving trivial conic structure? In this research, we have examined the complex aspect of the Heavy Quark potential, focusing on its dissociation at high temperatures and strong magnetic fields. Our work builds upon previous studies by introducing three distinct features: comprehensive calculations of Landau levels, a novel gauge boson propagator in a magnetized plasma, and an intricate, direction-dependent heavy quark potential. To showcase our advancements, we have generated detailed visualizations, such as heavy quark potential tomography and dissociation probability diagrams, at various temperature and magnetic field conditions. Our findings highlight how, in certain situations, heavy quark potential dissociation can occur due to magnetic field effects in one direction while remaining stable in perpendicular directions. Additionally, our research has demonstrated significant variations in dissociation probabilities among different Landau levels. Our research has vast implications for potential quark-gluon plasma studies and future particle collider experiments. Our predictions made here may be tested in the same way that those quark-gluon plasma properties are being measured in RHIC and LHC. Furthermore, our research has potential connections to the properties of superdense compact stars, specifically neutron stars, as their inherent magnetic fields could influence heavy quark potential dynamics. Our research has potential applications in the analysis of compact star properties via electromagnetic signals emitted during heavy quark states. Such signals could offer insights into magnetic field properties within these stars. Lastly, our work has left some queries unanswered. One of those is how heavy quark potential dynamics would behave when the magnetic field strength exceeds the critical value of 6.3 lions per square centimeter. To effectively answer complex questions, large language models need information about specific entities, but can't store all necessary knowledge themselves, so they rely on external sources like knowledge graphs to fill gaps. Our proposed solution, OREO-LM, includes a special layer that lets a language model work together with a knowledge graph to find the best answer, and in return, the language model becomes more accurate. By integrating OREO-LM with existing language models, such as RoBERTa and T5, we achieved record-breaking results and also got better explanations for the models' choices, thanks to the ability to infer new relationships between entities. Notably, our models are flexible and can be adapted to question answering, entity classification, and other tasks, and even do well when faced with questions that contain misleading information. Finally, we successfully applied these models to real-world data and achieved significant improvements. For example, our models produced an average 2.7% improvement in F1 score on the entity classification task, and up to 9.2% improvement in F1 score on question answering tasks, across five different datasets. We also found that the ability of these models to infer new relationships between entities resulted in an average 1.6% improvement in F1 score on entity classification tasks, and up to 4.8% improvement in F1 score on question answering tasks. These results are particularly notable because the ability of these models to infer new relationships between entities is particularly important when answering complex questions, and when working with large datasets, and we hope these results will encourage others to use similar models to improve their own results. Building upon expander graphs, high dimensional expanders play a vital role in theoretical computer science but unfortunately, there are only a few constructions available at present. Our research demonstrates that every high dimensional expander has a space-forming cover, a concept we defined, and furthermore, this cover can be constructed explicitly using only group actions, rendering the results applicable to groups with combinatorial properties, such as Cayley graphs. Integrating a technique in [Garcia, Koehler, Shiner, arXiv:1803.10113], we have also obtained a symmetric representation of the chromatic number of these space-forming covers. Recent advancements in language models have revealed the potential for outstanding zero-shot performance through cleverly crafted natural language prompts. However, creating effective prompts necessitates considerable trial and error. Consequently, there is a pressing need to determine which qualities of a prompt influence its efficacy. To this end, we have collected and standardized a diverse set of prompts designed for specific tasks and tested them on tasks for which they were not initially intended. Our quantitative analysis across multiple fixed choice datasets demonstrates that prompts containing multiple questions and those not referencing the model by name exhibit improved performance. While our findings are constrained to the fixed choice format, we anticipate that our observations hold value for other areas of natural language understanding. Additionally, we have released a flexible framework for automated prompt evaluation, encompassing a substantial collection of prompts for various tasks, including question answering, classification, translation, and more. This resource includes a wide range of prompts, including some that were utilized in our study, and can be utilized to validate new language models or to identify which prompts pose a challenge to current models. The code for our research, along with the dataset of evaluated prompts, can be found at https://github.com/alecmagnus/prompt_eval. This text investigates the Scrivannini-Touze $\mathscr{L}$-invariant for weight one systems and explains how this invariant ties into a broader pattern among coefficients of motive representations. Additionally, we outline a general method to calculate the $\mathscr{L}$-invariant for any Artin motive representation with weights that are divisible by two. We also compute the $\mathscr{L}$-invariant for the representation associated with the cubic motive $\mathrm{Mot}(\sqrt[3]{s}/\mathbb{Q})$. Such a representation has weights that are multiples of six, which motivates our proposed method. We further verify that the resulting value for $\mathscr{L}$ accurately matches Jannitz's formula for local factorization of the cubic discriminant. We expect our method to be applicable to a wide array of motives with weights that are multiples of a fixed integer greater than two. We also note that our central argument may be generalized to settings outside of motive representation systems with functional equations. We illustrate this by applying a similar idea to derive a closed-form expression for the Bernoulli number $B_{p,n}$. We also utilize this result to investigate properties of specific cubic fields, which we describe as $1.$ $\Q(\sqrt[3]{t})$ where $t$ represents the value of $3a^2+3b^2+3c^2-3$. We note that our investigation of the cubic fields does not rely on the previously mentioned results related to the motivic $\mathscr{L}$-invariant, which highlights the broad applicability of the generalized $\mathscr{L}$-invariant notion. Detecting complex multifrequency microwave (MW) electric fields is difficult 
due to interference from overlapping frequencies. Research using Rydberg 
atoms shows promise in MW radar and communications systems. Yet, the atoms are 
susceptible not only to desired signals, but also to interference from 
atomic interactions and environmental noise. To resolve these challenges, we've 
successfully implemented a Rydberg-atom-based approach combined with deep 
convolutional neural networks to analyze the atomic spectra. This technique has 
accurately extracted frequencies and amplitudes from MW signals, even when 
the signals are heavily obscured by noise. Notably, this method can identify 
frequencies within a frequency range of up to 10 F, which is a key benefit. 
Additionally, the method's effectiveness can be optimized by adjusting a 
dimensionless parameter, the Rydberg number. Experiments supporting the Rydberg 
atom approach may lead to its adoption in future quantum networks. However, 
significant technical hurdles must be addressed before its utilization. 

Keywords: Rydberg atoms, Multifrequency microwave signals, Deep convolutional 
neural networks, Quantum networks. 

Please note: The Rydberg states are generally discussed in the context of 
frequencies in MHz, whereas the Rydberg number (R) is typically discussed 
in the context of atomic energy levels and not frequencies. In this abstract, 
R and MW are used for clarity, but maintain their usual meanings. 

For editors: In this study, we utilize R ~ 1000, corresponding to Rydberg 
frequencies of approximately 100 MHz. However, R can take on a vast range, 
given its dependency on the atomic mass. For our specific atomic selection, R 
can reach up to 5000.

under Grant #DF20-05142.

quantum networks due to its potential to serve as a compact, mobile, and 
reconfigurable component. Furthermore, researchers are exploring the 
integration of Rydberg atoms with other quantum systems, including solid-state 
devices, optical fibers, and other atoms. As such, Rydberg atoms may play a 
key role in future quantum networks.

The LHC holds the record for the highest energy particle collisions, encompassing not only proton-proton and heavy ion interactions but also those of photons with photons and hadrons. This capability stems from the fact that protons and ions within the LHC possess an electromagnetic field, acting as a source of photons that can interact with other photons or hadrons. This phenomenon is observed in ultra-peripheral collisions (UPCs) that involve photons colliding with photons or hadrons. Researchers have recently utilized data from such UPCs at the LHC to gain insight into photon-proton interactions cross-sections at extremely high energies. Furthermore, the ALICE detector has recently analyzed forward J/psi production in lead-lead UPCs at 5.02 TeV, providing new measurements that include photoproduction cross-sections and an initial assessment of the photon-proton luminosity. These findings demonstrate an increase in the measured cross-section by a factor of more than 10 compared to previous experiments, revealing a strong correlation with the photon energy and nuclear thickness. Additionally, the data exhibit satisfactory agreement with the theoretical predictions based on the Glauber and VENUS/MPS models. To further understand nuclear interactions, the researchers are planning to accumulate up to twenty times the present data, paving the way for precise measurements of nuclear structure functions and photon-proton cross-sections at extremely high energies. It is anticipated that these measurements will provide significant insight into the behavior of photons interacting with matter, serving as a complementary supplement to data obtained from electron-proton colliders. The researchers are also exploring the potential for new discoveries, including the detection of dimuon pairs resulting from photoproduction and the measurement of rapidity distribution of the J/psi meson. The ongoing data collection is also enabling the study of nuclear phenomena at very low momentum transfers, providing an opportunity to verify and further investigate theoretical models such as the eikonal model. Furthermore, the researchers are examining the possibility of using the sampled data to extract nuclear form factors, offering a novel approach to doing so. To achieve these goals, the researchers are working on establishing a photon-proton luminosity function that accurately represents the characteristics of photon-proton interactions, incorporating the concepts of impact parameter and equivalent photon number. Additionally, the researchers are utilizing the measured data to verify and further understand theoretical models such as the VENUS/MPS model, which describes photon-proton interactions using the equivalent photon approximation, and the Glauber model, which accounts for the effects of nuclear interactions. This research explores using longer, typically five-second audio selections to complement visually captured moments. We introduce a conditional audio synthesis model that leverages these longer audio examples to learn a more robust, visually driven sound generation framework. Additionally, this paper delves into evaluating visually guided sound generation models using subjective assessment methods to gain deeper insight into their creative potential. It also addresses concerns related to model control, highlighting both the challenges and successful outcomes thus far. Finally, the study demonstrates the feasibility of generating visually linked sound effects using only brief video clips of approximately ten frames (3 seconds). In doing so, it establishes a strong foundation for the theoretical underpinnings of this sound effect learning method and provides a practical standard for future research to build upon. Recurrent neural networks have emerged as highly effective algorithms for processing sequential data, including natural languages, sounds, and time-series information. In contrast to conventional feed-forward networks, they incorporate a self-referential mechanism, allowing for the retention of temporal context and the sequential transmission of information. This architecture has enabled exceptional performance in a range of significant tasks such as natural language modeling, stock market forecasting, image description, speech recognition, machine translation, and object tracking. However, the process of training fully connected recurrent networks is complex, involving intricate gradient flow management. To address these challenges, numerous studies have been conducted. This article aims to provide an overview of recurrent neurons and their variations, as well as the techniques for efficiently training fully connected recurrent networks. An innovative solution presented in [1] serves as a foundation for the discussion, offering a simple and effective method for linking multiple recurrent units together and eliminating the associated memory limitations. A comprehensive flow is also proposed to streamline the training process. This paper delves into a Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular class of annular domains. Specifically, we examine a setup involving a larger open set $\Omega_0$, a smaller ball of radius $r$, and consider a first eigenvalue in this scenario where both the Steklov and Robin boundary conditions are imposed. We then analyze the main features of the eigenvalue and its associated eigenfunctions, as well as how the parameter $\beta$ and $r$ influence the behavior of the eigenvalue when they vary. When $\beta$ is positive, we establish that the eigenvalue undergoes an ascent before reaching its maximum at $\beta=1$, and using analytical methods, we find the exact asymptotic behavior of the eigenvalue as $r$ approaches $0$. We also show that the nodal lines of the eigenfunctions converge asymptotically onto a sphere of radius $r$ as $r$ tends towards $0$. When $\beta$ is negative, we demonstrate that the eigenvalue exhibits alternating patterns of increase and decrease, and we determine the exact asymptotic behavior of the eigenvalue as $r$ approaches $0$ and $r$ approaches infinity. Lastly, we find that the asymptotic locations of the eigenfunctions do not converge onto a specific surface but rather describe the geometry of the domain as $r$ tends towards either $0$ or $\infty$. Our analysis also sheds light on an interesting connection to Minkowski's theorem. We utilize a combination of scaling arguments, dimensionless analysis, and analytical methods to derive these results and findings. It is worth noting that the methods employed in this paper are distinct from our previous work on Robin eigenvalue problems, instead drawing upon new and innovative approaches. Additionally, although this research primarily focuses on understanding a theoretical eigenvalue in a complex geometric context, many of the analytical techniques and results may find practical applications in other problems involving both theoretical and applied mathematics. Furthermore, while this paper concentrates on Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problems, we anticipate that many of the techniques and results will also be applicable to co-Eigenvalues in both Steklov-Robin and other eigenvalue problems. Election manipulation through the alteration of voting district boundaries constitutes
a long-standing issue in democracy, yet detecting it has been challenging due to
the absence of clear analytical evidence. To address this concern, we developed a
method combining Markov Chain Monte Carlo and Simulated Annealing to quantify the
level of unfairness in a districting plan. Our results show the effectiveness of
this approach in a range of scenarios, particularly those without obvious biases. 
This application, incorporated into Territorial, an open-source tool for exploring
districting plans, enables users to analyze the fairness of any desired districting
plan or variation. As an example, we applied the method to the 2011 Texas redrawing
of voting district boundaries, revealing a high probability of unfair manipulation.
Furthermore, we explored the relationship between our method and Kern's compactness
measure, establishing a relationship between the fairness and compactness metrics. To
foster transparency and reproduce our findings, we publicly share the code and data
employed in our analysis. Finally, we suggest potential future developments, such
as incorporating the fairness method into optimization techniques for automated district
division. This research aims to contribute to the development of transparent and
fair voting procedures. To achieve this, we are making available a plugin for Territorial
called "Justice" that allows users to easily assess fairness in districting plans. 
This plugin is now integrated into Territorial as a standard feature. To promote
transparency, we are sharing the code used in our research. The Justice plugin is
currently available for download on our website at <https://justistricting.org/justice>. This research is a product of collaboration between the labs of

A novel defect detection approach for patterned fabric images utilizes a direction-sensitive feature descriptor, GHOG, which integrates Gabor and HOG to precisely locate defects. Since defects distort the fabric's uniform pattern, causing rank reduction in the image, low-rank decomposition can pinpoint the defect area. However, this method may fail if the decomposition process cannot recover the exact defect shape or if the defect area overlaps with the image border. To address these issues, we propose an efficient and accurate fabric defect detection framework. It begins with GHOG feature extraction to capture the direction-dependent spatial variations in the image. Next, the extracted features feed a support vector machine classifier to distinguish between defect and intact images. Utilizing low-rank decomposition, the fabricated training data can learn to separate intact and defect areas. This method is specifically designed for patterned fabric images and demonstrates superior accuracy compared to state-of-the-art techniques. To evaluate its effectiveness, we tested the proposed framework on a substantial dataset consisting of 36,800 images spanning various fabric types, defects, and backgrounds. Notably, this dataset is significantly larger and more diverse than existing benchmarks. Experimental outcomes confirm that our approach outperforms competing methods, yielding impressive cross-category accuracy rates of 97.93% and 95.33% for small and large defect sizes, respectively. Additionally, the proposed framework demonstrates robustness across different background intensities and fabric types. The extracted GHOG features and the low-rank decomposition-based method contribute to unique and informative feature representations, surpassing the performance of existing fabric defect detection techniques. To validate its practical value, we evaluated the detected defects and compared their shapes to those manually labeled by human experts, revealing close similarity. Furthermore, we successfully tested the proposed framework on real-world fabric roll images captured using a CMOS camera. These imaging conditions can degrade fabric appearance due to illumination non-uniformity, resulting in decreased performance. To mitigate these effects, we incorporated background subtraction into the framework, demonstrating improved accuracy and robustness. Notably, this modified approach yielded 93.33% cross-category accuracy rate, outperforming the baseline method. Consequently, the proposed framework emerges as a highly effective solution for accurate fabric defect detection, particularly when processing patterned images and large datasets. Its potential value extends to various industrial settings where automatic defect identification could boost productivity and quality control. The proposed framework has been made available on GitHub, enabling others to replicate the results and build upon this research. https://github.com/jaahmed/fabric_defect_detection. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 120 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly ten times.
Using cutting-edge technologies, TextWorldExpress can process over one million actions per second, while preserving the same intricate game elements that made the original games challenging and effective for testing agents. 
By pushing the boundaries of text-based game simulation speed, TextWorldExpress opens up new avenues for extensive training of robust agents using large datasets and multiple distributed GPUs. 
Our evaluation involves comparing the performance of three agents trained on different versions of our game, showcasing improved speed as the primary gain when processing larger datasets. 
Moreover, TextWorldExpress provides a versatile framework for custom game development, encompassing a substantial collection of game elements and actions, as well as dynamic environments, non-static objects, and realistic physics. 
Our research introduces the TextWorldExpress benchmark, a set of challenging text-based game challenges designed to assess virtual agents in tasks like solving complex problems and applying real-world knowledge. 
The benchmark comprises three distinct game types: puzzle-solving, where the focus lies on applying solvable principles, applying rules, and solving mysteries, respectively. 
Our evaluation compares the performance of three agents trained on different versions of our game, achieving varying levels of success, and highlights the difficulties encountered by agents when processing our game at one million actions per second. 
TextWorldExpress is now open-source and accessible at a designated repository for further collaboration and development.

Building on existing research, we developed a new algorithm to generate manipulability ellipsoids in tasks involving 3D point cloud processing. Unlike previous methods, which require ground truth data, our algorithm enables learning to generate these ellipsoids from unmarked point cloud data.
