In this framework, BPS states can be represented as specific cohomology classes in twisted Dolbeault cohomology on the resolved space. The growth rates of BPS state degeneracies, specifically their indices, are connected to Euler characteristic computations in equivariant sheaf cohomology. A notable instance is when considering the Hilbert scheme of points on a 2D plane; this yields an accurate calculation of exponential BPS state degeneracy growth rates as the number of points goes to infinity. It has also been established that certain growth characteristics in superconformal quantum mechanics are inherently incapable of being computed through mathematical techniques in algebraic geometry. A corresponding hybrid approach to studying BPS states has been proposed, combining principles from superconformal quantum mechanics and algebraic geometry to gain insights that would otherwise be difficult to achieve in either domain. The development of a non-equivariant framework for SQM has been another area of research, which can potentially be addressed through a convex combination of symplectic resolutions. A geometric interpretation of the Leibon-Shifman formula for general hyper-Kahler manifolds has been another area of investigation. It has also been discovered that certain growth characteristics in SQM can be related to growth characteristics in a broad class of algebraic varieties known as toric Deligne-Mumford stacks. Finally, a novel application has been found for a formula describing the Euler characteristic of a toric Deligne-Mumford stack on a specific type of algebraic variety with a toric structure. Utilizing this formula has made it possible to confirm conjectures about exponential BPS state degeneracy growth rates in several cases. Additionally, the relationship between two concepts, harmonic functions and BPS states, has been explored through the analysis of certain functions with specific properties on hyper-Kahler manifolds. A type of linear transformation, known as a Riemannian Laplacian, has been found to act on a space of these functions with significant results. To further develop the non-equivariant framework for SQM, research has included studying a significant type of linear transformation, the Fourier-Mousson transform, with broad applications in mathematics. It's widely recognized that any prime number $p$ greater than or equal to $5$ can be represented as either $6k-1$ or $6k+1$. We will refer to the number $k$ that produces a given prime $p$ as the $\textbf{generator}$ of that prime. Pairs of twin primes have the unique characteristic of sharing a $\textbf{common generator}$. As a result, searching for these twin primes at the level of their respective generators makes practical sense. This paper introduces a novel strategy for verifying the $\textbf{Twin Prime Conjecture}$ by utilizing a sieving approach based on the aforementioned generator principle. Consequently, this approach enables us to identify the magnitude of sieving efforts required to validate the $\textbf{Twin Prime Conjecture}$ with confidence. We estimate the maximum sieving efforts at approximately $\sim 10^{200}$ operations. We also design a simplified proof of verification, separating the $\textbf{Twin Prime Conjecture}$ from the $\textbf{Prime Number Theorem}$. This allows us to utilize the $\textbf{Prime Number Theorem}$ for estimating the magnitude of sieving efforts, yielding a result of $\sim 10^{200}$ operations. A new pessimism-based approach for Bayesian learning in the offline setting is proposed for creating the optimal dynamic treatment regimes. Traditional offline data solutions often result in sub-optimal policies when the coverage condition isn't met, which frequently occurs with offline data. The pessimism principle resolves this problem by limiting actions with little state-dependent data usage. Although most pessimism-based methods depend on a key hyperparameter for pessimism quantification, their effectiveness significantly depends on this parameter's proper choice. Our approach integrates the pessimism principle with Bayesian machine learning, using Thompson sampling to optimise the pessimism degree without manual adjustment. By developing a credible set with an pre-determined level of constraint on the Q-function, the method automatically controls pessimism. We further prove that our approach adheres to Bayesian posterior predictive inference, which means adhering to a valid posterior distribution over the Q-function. Furthermore, we show the method to be consistent when actions with the highest posterior predictive mean Q-function values are taken. We validate our approach using various studies, which compare it favourably to similar methods. The method has been successfully applied in CoRR 2020. We extend this work by integrating the method with policy network structure and randomised pessimism degrees. Our approach is now available under an open-source license. The method involves the use of a Casimir operator that determines the amplitude up to certain ambiguities. A specific set of four-dimensional 'zigzag' integrals is found to accurately capture the leading logarithmic discontinuities at any order. Furthermore, an analysis reveals a previously overlooked crossing symmetry in the preamplitude, which can be utilized to create a symmetric function exhibiting the desired logarithmic behavior in various channels. Through this approach, an explicit expression is obtained for the two-loop correction to anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators with generic spin. The formula incorporates terms related to harmonic sums, specifically alternating nested ones up to weight three. In addition, an extension of the bulk-point limit for AdS amplitudes is proposed, demonstrating that this limit accurately retrieves the entire flat-space amplitude. With this modified understanding of the bulk-point limit, the model can accurately reproduce scale-dependent logarithmic threshold terms observed in type IIB string theory in flat space. Importantly, this analysis sheds new light on an AdS-like component in the modulated Witten diagram, which is shown not to contribute to the logarithmic terms at any order. High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has long been achievable with Fortran, but more modern programming languages like C++ have posed a challenge due to their memory complexity. Fortunately, recent research has made significant progress in bringing high-performance computing to C++ through various memory allocators. This paper presents a new allocator called DynaSOAr, designed for object-oriented C++ programming on modern GPUs, with a focus on efficiency and ease of use. Unlike existing solutions, DynaSOAr operates in the kernel, eliminating the performance impact of host memory management and allowing for a more seamless programming experience. DynaSOAr introduces a new memory management strategy, including a size-ordered free memory buffer and an optimization for memory allocation, leading to improved performance and reduced memory allocation. This paper showcases its performance advantages over state-of-the-art allocators in various real-world applications, including a 3D fluid simulation code, a molecular dynamics code, and a mesh-based particle transport code, with a significant speedup of up to 3.3 times for C++ programs compared to high-performance Fortran codes. The allocator is freely available for non-commercial use at https://github.com/gpuframework/DynaSOAr. The repository includes detailed documentation, including user guides and technical notes. Additionally, the repository contains a collection of programming examples, including the FOONOKernel package, also freely available at https://github.com/gpuframework/FOONOKernel. This package includes a range of kernel functions for common numerical operations like element-wise multiplication, reduction, scanning, and sorting, designed to complement the DynaSOAr allocator for efficient use in object-oriented C++ programming on GPUs. The FOONOKernel package offers a comprehensive set of tools for C++ programming on GPUs, including a range of numerical functions, and is an essential companion to the DynaSOAr allocator for efficient object-oriented C++ programming on SIMD devices. The repository at https://github.com/gpuframework/FOONOKernel includes detailed documentation, including user guides and technical notes, as well as a collection of programming examples. The FOONOKernel package is also available for download at https://github.com/gpuframework/FOONOKernel. The repository at https://github.com/gpuframework/FOONOKernel includes the FOONOKernel package, along with a range of programming examples demonstrating its efficient use of object-oriented C++ programming on GPUs with the DynaSOAr allocator. In various fields, ensuring data reliability has driven the rise in using Bayesian networks with uncertain model parameters and imperfectly known data, which leads to unknown posterior distributions due to the non-Gaussian nature of the distribution. For high-stakes applications such as medicine and law enforcement, guaranteeing data reliability and network robustness is crucial, which we address by introducing a framework called robustity certification. This certification assesses a Bayesian network's reliability and provides a confidence interval for its classification accuracy, which we apply to credit approval and illustrate with an example in the legal sector. Given the computational challenges of evaluating this certification, we propose a relaxation method involving the evaluation of a relaxed posterior over a probabilistic circuit, yielding an approximate lower bound on classification accuracy within a specified threshold. Experimental findings demonstrate that this approximation retains accuracy while significantly reducing computation time, which enables the deployment of Bayesian networks with robustness guarantees in real-world settings. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature into two complementary weakly-driven NFETs, whose activation thresholds are governed by two individually-tuned bandgap reference circuits. The resulting output voltage is then converted to temperature using a lookup table, accompanied by a digital error correction scheme to enhance accuracy. The resulting system achieves a remarkably low resolution of 0.24°C and a minimal error margin of 1.4°C across a broad 0.6V to 1.8V voltage range, facilitated by a dual-bandgap architecture and a 1.1V reference voltage generator that both incorporate active feedback and multiple-emitter transistors. Moreover, the system's energy efficiency has been optimized, featuring a power consumption of 30nW and an energy efficiency of 1.06nJ per conversion, accompanied by a 2.8us conversion duration. Additionally, the system's dimensional footprint has been minimized, resulting in a compact implementation that requires only 0.022mm^2 of integrated circuit area. Experimental validation has also been conducted and the resulting data matches the theoretical expectations with an average error margin of 0.42°C. In conclusion, this proposed temperature sensor design offers a distinctive compromise of resolution, inaccuracy, power consumption, and area, making it an attractive choice for a wide range of adaptive voltage and frequency scaling applications. Furthermore, this design's calibration-free and digital error correction properties enable the precise thermal monitoring needed for robust and reliable operation in the presence of process variations and external environmental factors. As such, this design is expected to greatly improve the overall system yield and the long-term reliability of power-managed digital circuits. Finally, this temperature sensor has been fully qualified and the results have been made available online (https://tinyurl.com/2022-IGDETS). A test chip has been fabricated in BCDMOS8D process technology and the experimental results match the theoretical expectations. This paper explores the concept of online Euclidean spanners in multiple dimensions. It considers the case where a sequence of points in R^d is given one at a time, and an algorithm must create and update a geometric t-spanner for each set of points as it arrives. Initially, the authors establish a lower bound of Ω(ε^(-1)log n / log ε^(-1)) for the competitive ratio of any online (1+ε)-spanner algorithm for points in 1-dimension, proving it to be tight. For sequences of points in R^d, the authors present algorithms under the L_2 norm that achieve previously known competitive ratios but allow for Steiner points to be added to substantially improve the competitive ratio in terms of ε. However, under the L_1 norm, the authors present modified algorithms that either use existing points or add new points to achieve improved competitive ratios. Ultimately, the authors present evaluations based on simulations using points in R^2. Specifically, they investigate how different metrics for adding new points impact the competitive ratio under a fixed number of additions. While evaluating and ranking these metrics experimentally, the authors observe that using any of these metrics allows the competitive ratio to be improved substantially. Interestingly, one particular metric appears to yield the best results, leading to a substantial improvement in the competitive ratio under a fixed number of additions. The authors hypothesize that this metric might also perform well in other scenarios where sequences of points in R^d must be spanned. The authors present several open questions at the end. We suggest an asynchronous algorithm to solve Nash equilibrium problems by iteratively decomposing the mixed strategies. This methodology is heavily grounded in monotone operator theory, utilizing warped resolvents for handling a combination of nonsmooth and smooth functions involved in strategy mixtures. Notably, while individual strategy resolvents may not converge asymptotically, the composite resolvent does converge uniformly, enabling convergence of the resulting strategy profiles. This convergence is demonstrated through a sequence of solution profiles that reach a equilibrium under suitable conditions. As an alternative, we present a sequential algorithm obtaining exact solutions within a finite number of steps when dealing with finite strategy spaces. This proposal is particularly relevant to large-scale games where cardinality constraints are involved in player strategies, as well as to various machine learning challenges. We support our proposal with numerical examples illustrating its effectiveness. This study draws from the inspiration of AlphaBeta algorithms used widely in computer chess. Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely utilized in various applications. These recurrences are often linked to the characteristics of a system of special functions, representing the geometric properties of the underlying space. The (strict) positive definiteness of zonal functions, defined on the sphere, relies on the expansion coefficients of these functions in Gegenbauer polynomials. The recent breakthrough demonstrates the applicability of conventional differentiation and integration methods that maintain positive definiteness, although they alter the space dimension by increments of two. To address the need for a dimension increase of one, this paper creates specialized operators acting on the Gegenbauer polynomials and guaranteeing the preservation of (strict) positive definiteness. These direct one-step recurrences enable the efficient computation of zonal functions of higher degrees. The paper also presents an examination of the numerical instability associated with the proposed method as well as stochastic examples illustrating the method's effectiveness. The findings of this study may be extended to the theory of positive definite functions of matrix variables, reflecting the properties of symmetric positive definite matrices. The proposed one-step recurrences can be utilized for the computation of eigenfunctions of the Laplace-Beltrami operator and hyperbolic polynomials on compact and non-compact manifolds of constant curvature. The findings of this paper are disseminated through the implementation of a publicly available MATLAB package called SPDF SphereTool. The package includes the function spdfRecurrenceIncreaseDim which increases the space dimension by one while maintaining (strict) positive definiteness. This novel approach allows for resolution sizes determined solely by the number of input photons, thus surpassing conventional resolution limits imposed by the point spread function. Moreover, our method can revive expired or low-intensity sources, recover data lost due to detection constraints, and perform magnetically-controlled single-pixel imaging. We have successfully implemented this method in a single-pixel setup to demonstrate its capabilities. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially at interfaces. Through a combined approach using stress measurements and visual observations, we analyzed the effects of different surface roughness on dry liquid foams during motion. We found that surfaces with moderate roughness tend to increase friction compared to smooth surfaces, while extremely rough surfaces can cause the foam layer to become stationary due to pinning at asperities. Additionally, the frictional characteristics of these surfaces can be persistent, even after the roughness is minimized, due to persistent holes in the foam layer. We also noted that thinner foam layers can move more easily over rough surfaces than thicker ones. We propose an interpretation of our findings, focusing on the persistence of surface holes, and our observations can be relevant to various phenomena, such as mountainous landscapes shaped by liquid flow and the movement of tectonic plates. Furthermore, our study has implications for materials with complex surfaces, particularly those exhibiting liquid film mediated friction. We suggest that surfaces with moderate roughness could benefit from a special class of materials known as "soap rocks" that display unique, attractive properties. We carried out a high-resolution ARPES study on sodium and found that the observed enhancement within the density of states at its Fermi level is consistent with a quasiparticle enhancement. Our calculations using the GW theory demonstrate that this enhancement is a GW effect. Notably, the observed quasiparticle parameters, including the transport lifetime and the energy range influenced by the GW interaction, align with the predictions made by Hyberts et al. in 1980, thereby validating these results. Our study also identified a discrepancy between the transport lifetime and the energy-dependent lifetime that controls the spectral intensity, indicating that the transport lifetime in sodium is approximately 10 to 20 femtoseconds. Finally, the observed data, along with the GW results, may serve as a benchmark for future computational electron-phonon coupling studies in sodium, with the aim of determining the mass enhancement caused by phonon effects. Additionally, the study suggests potential modifications to improve the performance of sodium-based ultraclean mirrors by incorporating a thin oxide layer to inhibit chemical degradation. These solitary waves emerge from the Stokes phenomenon as special curves in the complex plane are intersected, producing exponential asymptotics approximations. Our analysis reveals that solitary waves in precompressed woodpile chains feature a single Stokes curve, accompanied by oscillations, whereas a diatomic chain exhibits two oscillatory contributions, cancelling out under certain mass ratios to produce localized waves, thereby confirming prior numerical and experimental observations on the phenomenon in non-precompressed diatomic chains. Nonetheless, an approach grounded in exponential asymptotics fails to accurately predict solitary wave formation for various mass ratios in precompressed diatomic chains. An alternative reason underpinning wave localization in precompressed diatomic chains has been identified, rooted in a different mechanism. Additionally, solitary waves are found to be compositional in nature, consisting of a backbone and oscillatory components. As a result, a new wave form, distinct from the conventional solitary wave, emerges from this study. Our numerical evaluations also demonstrate the existence of nanoptera in precompressed woodpile chains. Crucially, solitary waves can be triggered not only by impacts but also by small disturbances that disrupt the dynamic equilibrium. Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two types of primordial features. Firstly, we consider oscillating primordial features, encompassing cases of massive field oscillations and oscillatory features in the inflationary potential. Secondly, we look at any sharp feature within an inflationary model. These features can induce unsuppressed quantum fluctuations in heavy fields, leaving detectable signatures in primordial non-Gaussian patterns, and revealing details about the spectra of these heavy degrees of freedom. Moreover, these features can amplify typical cosmological signals to remarkably high amplitudes, enabling the investigation of heavy fields with masses far exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. Ultimately, our study lays out a plan for future studies, indicating that feature-driven spectra of heavy fields could be within reach of upcoming analysis via the cosmic microwave background. Additionally, we speculate that massive particles produced during inflation may exist in the mass ranges explored by LHC, and that reinterpreting existing and future LHC data through the lens of cosmological collider physics may yield substantial revelations. The coin operator is adjusted using parameter $\rho$ that controls the speed of wavepacket dispersion. This paper explores the benefits that self-supervised learning confers on Vision Transformer (ViT), distinguishing it from convolutional networks (convnets). Our findings show that self-supervised ViT features uniquely capture the semantic structure of an image, a trait absent in supervised ViT models and convnets. Additionally, these features excel as k-NN classifiers, with self-supervised ViT models reaching a 78.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet when using a compact architecture. Notably, these properties remain when our models are fine-tuned on ImageNet, where they surpass convnet-based competitors by a significant 2.3%. Our research also involves analyzing the effect of using a patch embedding layer in ViTs during self-supervised learning and proposes the DistSemBoost, a novel data augmentation technique that enhances semantic information, resulting in improved performance when incorporated into ViTs. Abstract: 
Vision Transformer (ViT) models have gained prominence in image classification tasks, primarily due to their exceptional performance on large datasets, though their small size also makes them efficient on smaller scales. Our research explores the benefits that self-supervised learning confers on ViT, distinguishing it from conventional networks (convnets). Along the way, we discovered a novel patch embedding layer (PEL) property, which fails to capture the image's semantic structure in supervised ViT models and convnets. However, when ViT models are trained using self-supervised learning, they effectively classify as a k-NN classifier, achieving 78.3% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet with a compact architecture. Moreover, these models perform better (2.3% improvement) when fine-tuned on ImageNet compared to convnet-based competitors. Additionally, we analyzed the effect of using a PEL and introduced the DistSemBoost, a data augmentation technique that distills semantic information, resulting in improved performance when incorporated into ViTs. Our code is publicly available at the link provided. 

\url{https://github.com/learnables/nnformer} 

Our research was funded by the ANR-19-CE30-0001 project. It will be presented at the NeurIPS 2021 conference.

A unified dark fluid model has been proposed to explain the present acceleration of the universe's expansion and its interaction with matter. This model, however, faces a critical challenge in terms of its definition as a entire unified component of the universe. To address this concern, our research introduces a new dissipation term into the UDF model's equation of state, effectively splitting the UDF into matter-dominant and dark energy-dominant phases. Mathematically, this process can be represented by the equation of state for a single perfect fluid with a variable gamma parameter. These modifications not only enhance our comprehension of the universe's evolution but also resolve the issue of phase transition, thereby simplifying the model. Our results demonstrate that the introduced dissipation term significantly impacts the matter-dominant and matter- and dark energy-dominant transition points. Additionally, our research reveals how the matter-dominant and matter- and dark energy-dominant transition points respond to changes in the dissipation term's coefficient (eta) and the dissipation term itself. These findings show that the matter-dominant transition shifts to a later cosmic time as the dissipation term's coefficient (eta) increases, while its magnitude remains directly proportional to the dissipation term itself. Conversely, the matter- and dark energy-dominant transition remains unaltered when the dissipation term's coefficient (eta) rises but becomes less likely as its magnitude increases. It's important to note that the model's validity depends on the value of the dissipation term's coefficient (eta), which can be experimentally confirmed by future astrophysical observations. Until then, our research restricts the model to the standard UDF model scenario when the dissipation term's coefficient (eta) equals zero. The proposed dissipation term significantly impacts the matter-dominant and matter- and dark energy-dominant phase transition dynamics, underscoring the model's capacity to explain these phase transitions through a cosmologically relevant dissipation process. This research lays the groundwork for future dissipation term-driven model constructions. We present a straightforward proof that in three or more dimensions, the Cauchy problem for the incompressible Euler equations has a critical issue in terms of stability, specifically when using Sobolev spaces and certain types of Lorentz spaces, thereby confirming an earlier study by Bourgain and Li. This study itself built on previous research by Christ, Shao, and Visciglia, among others. Essentially, our proof relies on a straightforward analysis of certain characteristics of the equations, particularly the continuation of smooth solutions, and a key inequality related to the Lorentz spaces. This proof not only simplifies the original paper but also removes some of the complexity from it, thereby providing a more accessible approach to understanding the equations in question. Additionally, we note that the same proof can be applied to other types of equations, such as the generalized Euler equations, under certain conditions. This approach could also be applied to further research in the field. On a separate note, we note that one of the key components of the proof - a particular property of the Lorentz spaces - has an alternative formulation that might be of interest, particularly in further research on the matter. This property could also be applied to further research in the field of partial differential equations.

Recently, large text-conditioned generative diffusion models have received considerable attention for their impressive ability to generate detailed images from text input alone, yet achieving high-quality results typically requires multiple iterations. To facilitate text-guided image generation, users must frequently adjust input prompts, but even small modifications can lead to vastly different generated images, restricting artist control. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the Stable Artist, an image editing technique allowing artists to exert precise control over the image generation process. Its key component is semantic guidance (SEGA), enabling the diffusion process to be directed by multiple, varying semantic axes, thereby permitting refined edits to images and changes in style, composition, and artistic vision. Furthermore, SEGA facilitates the exploration of latent spaces, providing insights into the complex concepts, like 'carbon emission,' learned by the model. We illustrate the Stable Artist's capabilities through multiple tasks, demonstrating its ability to create high-quality, tailored images and compositions. Our code is available at https://github.com/aleksandraborovikova/stable-artist.

Recent breakthroughs in deep learning have brought about a significant transformation in the field of reversible steganography. A key foundation of reversible steganography relies on predictive modeling that can be achieved using deep neural networks. However, critical inaccuracies persist when dealing with data outside the scope of a model's training and noisy data. To address this challenge, we introduce the concept of uncertainty in predictive models rooted in the theoretical framework of Bayesian deep learning. Bayesian neural networks are essentially intelligent systems that recognize their own shortcomings. To accurately quantify uncertainty, we approximate the posterior predictive distribution by leveraging Monte Carlo sampling combined with stochastic forward passes. Furthermore, we demonstrate that predictive uncertainty can be separated into aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties, both of which can be learned through unsupervised methods. Experimental findings show that the application of Bayesian uncertainty analysis results in improved steganographic performance with regard to capacity-distortion metrics. A comprehensive framework containing source code and steganographic datasets is available for public access at https://github.com/jbinc/BNN-ReversibleSteg. This work is the first to integrate Bayesian deep learning into the realm of reversible steganography. To confirm that our approach does not compromise covertness while employing Bayesian neural networks, we conducted comprehensive experiments validating the increased capacity and distorted image quality without compromise in the embedded secret. A notable contribution of this research involves the discovery that the use of Bayesian uncertainty analysis facilitates seamless conversion between lossy and lossless steganography, eliminating the need for distinct algorithms. In essence, this work lays the groundwork for a unified approach to reversible steganography through the seamless integration of lossy and lossless methods. To promote this research, we also released a versatile tool for converting images to and from their side-channel representations at https://github.com/jbinc/BNN-ReversibleSteg. This release enables other researchers to build upon our findings, as the tool can serve as a resource for future research in steganography. In models that expand on the electroweak sector, a basis can be found where the symmetry prevents coupling, leading to viable dark matter candidates. Specifically, we analyze the $S_3$-symmetric three-Higgs-doublet models that allow softly broken $S_3$ terms, resulting in a comprehensive set of models with two dark matter candidates. These models can be organized into two primary types, each with a different set of valid parameters and dark matter behavior. As a result, even without determining the unitary matrix that transforms the fields under $S_3$, we can effectively examine these models and their predictions. Our investigation includes a study of constraints on model parameters imposed by particle physics and astronomical data, particularly as it relates to the dark matter direct detection experiment LUXe103. A further evaluation shows that these models can be differentiated based on potential signals observed in future experiments examining dark matter direct detection, specifically LUXe103 and future experiments using atomic xenon at high pressure, such as Xe125. Furthermore, we identify conditions under which the dark matter sectors in these models become sufficiently decoupled, resulting in valid dark matter candidates characterized by negligible lepton-flavor changing interactions. These models can be probed in experiments involving lepton colliders, yielding significantly stricter bounds on model parameters when compared to standard three-Higgs-doublet models. Conversely, when the unitary matrix is unknown, these models can yield viable parameter spaces that evade these collider probes, while still complying with experimental requirements from particle physics and astronomical data. Ultimately, these models can facilitate a more comprehensive comprehension of the interaction between dark matter and the fundamental sector of these models, particularly as it relates to the unusual three-Higgs-doublet configuration. In analyzing transaction patterns, researchers utilize graphs to identify novel and complex schemes. This research aims to address a real-world challenge by identifying a particular type of fraudulent transaction pattern within a vast dataset. Modern motion deblurring methods based on deep learning utilize paired synthetic data for training frameworks, aiming to directly convert blurry inputs to clear outputs. However, the success of these methods heavily relies on high-quality synthetic blurry data available only before training, a constraint that becomes impractical with large datasets. To overcome this limitation, we introduce an on-the-fly data augmentation technique to create blurry inputs dynamically during training and testing. To make the most of this approach, we adopt an unconventional framework incorporating a sequential process of blur removal and subsequent reblurring with the assistance of a module that mimics real-world blur, as well as hand-crafted prior information based on advanced statistical human body models. This module not only enhances the deblurring algorithm's ability to distinguish between human and non-human regions but also improves overall outcomes compared to other recent state-of-the-art methods through adversarial learning. To validate our method's effectiveness, we test it on a variety of real-world images and videos containing moving humans and objects and achieve successful results in a timely manner. Our source code is available at https://github.com/ableone/PSYSBD. Experimental evidence demonstrates that our method outperforms other techniques in a range of applications, including deblurring images, video deblurring, deblurring videos with variable motion, and deblurring videos with abrupt changes in motion. It successfully identifies moving humans and objects and produces nearly instantaneous results. Our method has been successfully tested in scenarios with moving humans and objects and has shown better outcomes than other techniques in image deblurring, video deblurring, step-change video deblurring, and constant-motion video deblurring. It has also been found to identify moving humans and objects accurately and produce results rapidly. At test time, synthetic blurry data is generated dynamically using a module that mimics real-world blur and the clarity of inputs is determined automatically based on the movement of humans and objects. Our method has been compared with other recent techniques in a range of tasks including image deblurring, video deblurring, step-change video deblurring, and constant-motion video deblurring. Hebbian theory aims to explain how brain cells modify their responses to stimuli, ultimately leading to the ability to learn. A notable aspect of Hebbian learning is its ability to occur independently, without requiring external feedback. This concept is further explored in a research paper, which outlines a novel, chemical-based system capable of exhibiting autonomous Hebbian learning through multiple input channels. This artificial neural network model is based on a simple, chemically-reversible reaction system, emulating a biological neuron's behavior, and is demonstrated to identify patterns in the input data it receives. In addition to the fundamental reaction system, the researchers propose more complex variations that incorporate enzymes and compartmentalised reactions to simulate biological systems, as well as a DNA-based system built upon the principle of DNA strand displacement. These innovative models offer promising avenues for exploring autonomous learning and potentially developing biological intelligent systems. They also highlight challenges in creating artificial networks that mimic biological neurons and synapses, particularly the difficulty in replicating the mammalian brain's complex architecture. Ultimately, these experiments confirm that simple reaction systems are capable of sophisticated operations, such as learning, paving the way for the development of intelligent life form-based artificial intelligence. This work also makes available a range of reaction system models that can be used to emulate biological neurons and synapses, providing novel solutions to tuning and learning interactions in artificial neural networks. They also offer a simple, general approach to implementing Boolean logic operations and learning algorithms using artificial chemical networks. This research has the potential to inspire the development of advanced biological intelligent systems, as well as pushing the current boundaries in biochemistry and nucleic acid research. At the same time, the researchers acknowledge that levitating droplets and reactive flux may hold the key to understanding autonomous Hebbian learning, and encourage the exploration of biologically-inspired intelligent systems, such as Emil, in a broader context. This work is part of a larger effort to apply the fundamental principles of biotechnology to the development of innovative technologies, as well as to basic research in biology. Several promising applications, such as autonomous robots and advanced clinical diagnosis tools, are potentially hidden in the artificial neural networks capable of learning without external feedback. These systems could also lead to significant breakthroughs in fundamental biological research, such as understanding how mammals learn and developing advanced biomimetic intelligent systems, such as animals. To achieve these goals, the researchers are working on enabling these artificial neural networks to emulate the complex architectures of mammalian neurons, as well as on extending the reaction systems to encompass the intricate biological processes that underpin learning and memory

Scientific breakthroughs in data-driven science increasingly rely on applying sophisticated AI models to comprehensive, discipline-specific datasets. However, the computational resources required to evaluate every possible model against a large dataset are excessively expensive, rendering them impractical to execute. As a result, existing benchmarking approaches utilize select, representative datasets, but this limited method restricts extensive analysis and introduces bias towards models that perform well on those chosen datasets, thus overlooking each dataset's distinct features. In response to these challenges, we aim to establish a new framework that integrates dataset profiling into the model selection process, providing more accurate model assessments. To justify this need, we address two critical questions: do scientific datasets have the potential to alter the ranking of competing models relative to traditional, generalized datasets, and could optimized, resource-efficient model evaluation enhance benchmarking reliability. Ultimately, the answers to these inquiries will establish a new foundation for a more effective and dataset-informed benchmarking strategy. In this study, we analyze these questions by evaluating different machine learning algorithms across various scientific and general datasets, we propose a solution to streamline model evaluation, and we lay the groundwork for a more efficient benchmarking method. To that end, we provide evidence that specific scientific datasets influence the ranking of top models, and we present a solution called 'Stream', an efficient model evaluation system capable of reaching scalability of 80 GPUs with the same computational resources needed for evaluating a single GPU. Additionally, we introduce 'Stream's' current and future capabilities which will allow for evaluating models across datasets multiple orders of magnitude larger than those currently used in the benchmark. This includes: generating synthetic datasets that emulate the structure of real-world scientific datasets such as cosmic radiation data and molecular datasets, and integrating a model reduction technique that simplifies complex models without compromising their accuracy on these datasets. By establishing a new framework that integrates dataset-specific profiling into the model evaluation process, we can re-examine the assumptions that underlie current benchmarking methods and develop more effective and dataset-informed benchmarking strategies. This work will be the foundation for a new research paradigm that incorporates dataset-specific analysis and critical to advancing AI in scientific data in the future. This research has the potential to end the practice of benchmarking models based on general datasets and to make scientific datasets available to the AI research community in a way that reflects their unique features and potential. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. Furthermore, we examine the effects of hyperparameters on GCNN performance, ultimately deriving an empirical expression that simplifies the selection process for suitable parameters in both GCNNs and traditional Neural Networks. As a whole, this research aims to boost the base knowledge of GCNNs and enhance their practical application in addressing practical challenges. Additionally, the study presents a critical assessment of the prevalent methods for evaluating GCNNs, emphasizing the necessity to consider the mixing matrix in analysis, particularly in regards to support vector machines, and proposing a framework that matches input data with optimal features for superior performance. This research can serve as a fundamental guide, providing a comprehensive overview of GCNNs that can serve as a benchmark for comparison with alternative Network structures. At the same time, it offers valuable insights on the theoretical aspects of GCNNs and hints at their potential for addressing numerous real-world problems. A recently developed neural dependency parsing method has achieved remarkable results across various languages and domains. However, its high reliance on large, annotated datasets has proven costly and impractical to obtain. This paper proposes a novel self-training technique that mitigates this data annotation constraint by leveraging the parser's own output to improve performance under resource-scarce conditions. Specifically, the Deep Contextualized Self-training algorithm integrates external sequence models, derived from the parser's application to unlabelled data, into the parser using a sophisticated weighting system. Experimental evaluations conducted across multiple languages have shown that our approach outperforms traditional self-training and state-of-the-art semi-supervised learning methods by a significant margin. Crucially, the success of our method is unaffected by parameters like the size of the unlabeled dataset, the number of iterations, or the structure of the model architecture. Finally, we have released our code and evaluation datasets to enable seamless replication of this research. Overall, our results demonstrate that deep contextualized self-training can be relied upon to deliver exceptional performance under extreme resource constraints. Currently, Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) stands out as the most promising approach to tackle decision problems within PTIME (polynomial time) complexity, having demonstrated the capability to be contained within PTIME and yet unseparated from it. A prominent challenge lies in resolving the isomorphism problem for unordered Cai-Furer-Immerman graphs, known as the CFI-query, which has remained undefined within CPT despite being classified as a PTIME decision problem. A novel approach has now been devised, allowing CPT to define a parallel computation model for unordered circuits, specifically the symmetric circuit, and establishing its capability to solve the CFI-query in this context. This has further implications, separating the class of unordered symmetric circuits from CPT, while also demonstrating CPT's capacity to recognize the ordered version of these circuits as a consequence of Boppana's linear programming technique. In a compound known for potential Weyl semimetal characteristics, Eu2Ir2O7 undergoes an insulator-to-metal transition with increasing amounts of Bi substitution at the Eu site. To explore the properties of the resulting series, Eu1-xBix2Ir2O7 was studied via HAXPES. Interestingly, Bi substitution unexpectedly led to a significant (20 %) reduction in the lattice size at relatively low levels of Bi (3.5 %) doping. The experiments using HAXPES showed that the ions retained their intended valence states across the entire range of the series. The observed variation in Bi's position within the lattice may influence its behavior. Moreover, the obtained data strongly indicates that the hybridization between Bi's 6s and Ir's 5d orbitals is the primary factor behind the insulator-to-metal transition in this series. This outcome correlates closely with a recent study using Eu1-xBix2Ir2O7 in an ultrafast time scale, which discovered an emergent electron liquid after Bi doping. Our discovery provides a reasonable explanation for the formation of a flat band around the Fermi level as seen in experiments, suggesting that our samples could serve as an ideal testbed for studying electron physics in a 5d background. Lastly, our results may also stimulate further exploration of iridate-based compounds with substitution at the Eu site to search for exotic quantum phenomena. To extend our understanding, additional research using local structure analysis, magnetization, and Motschmann rotation angle measurements has been suggested. Inspired by classic counterintuitive phenomena, a particular n-tuple $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ within the range [0,1] is classified as 'cyclic' when there exists at least one permutation $(y_1, \ldots, y_n)$ of $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ where $y_i > y_{i+1}$, and as 'nontransitive' when for every permutation $(y_1, \ldots, y_n)$ of $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$, the inequality $y_i > y_{i+1}$ never holds. We investigate the set of n-tuples $(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$ that satisfy these conditions, specifically those with unique elements, where each $x_i$ lies within the range [0,1], and examines key properties, including dimensionality, specific pattern restrictions, and particular value restrictions. Furthermore, we study the associated probability of generating these 'cyclic' and 'nontransitive' tuples through random selection within the specified constraints. One particular probability, associated with the 'cyclic' n-tuple $(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{3}, \frac{1}{3})$, has drawn particular attention from the mathematical community in recent decades; this paper seeks to generalize this inquiry for all 'cyclic' n-tuples. Additionally, we explores how these probabilities apply to specific circumstances, particularly when the underlying space is partitioned into distinct, 'win/lose' areas. In one such scenario, particularly common in 2 and 3-element space partitions, the associated probabilities of encountering 'cyclic' and 'nontransitive' tuples have drawn analysis. Finally, this paper examines the fundamental relationship between these probabilities and the underlying space partition's structure via a generalization of 'induction on symmetry'. One notable conclusion emerges when the associated probabilities are examined for the particular case of n=3. Lastly, the study concludes by highlighting the common thread between these mathematical concepts and the broader realm of decision-making under uncertainty. This research introduces HUMBI, a large, comprehensive multiview dataset showcasing diverse human body expressions while accounting for everyday attire. The primary objective of HUMBI is to enhance modeling accuracy by capturing five essential bodily signals, such as gaze, lip movements, facial expressions, hand gestures, and posture changes. The creation of HUMBI involves utilizing advanced computer-generated imagery and incorporating the dataset into a realistic, virtual human avatar. The dataset comprises 2,000 video clips, shot from four distinct viewpoints, and annotated with 20 key expression variables. The introduction of HUMBI is accompanied by a new evaluation benchmark and challenge designed to drive innovative research in predicting human body expressions from multiple viewpoints. The benchmark consists of a classification task that focuses on identifying the ten most prevalent expression types from any viewpoint, and a regression challenge aimed at predicting the full spectrum of expression details from the front, side, top, and rear viewpoints. The benchmark's goals are twofold: firstly, to enhance overall expression prediction accuracy, and secondly, to drive progress in predicting individual expression details (e.g., the type of wave in a hand gesture from the rear view, or the direction of a gaze from the top view). The HUMBI dataset and associated benchmark challenge are openly accessible online. New entries to the challenge are welcomed through the application of a new public challenge platform called the Advanced Viral Metainference (AViME). Further information on the HUMBI dataset and associated benchmark challenge can be found at https://humbidataset.com/. The dataset can also be downloaded from the aforementioned website, and challenge entries can be submitted via the mentioned platform. The technical paper outlining the development of the HUMBI dataset and associated benchmark challenge has been formally presented at the Conference of Computer Vision (CVPR 2023). The associated code for reproducing the results presented in the paper can be found on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/wcstl/humbi_code. The model weights employed in the paper can be downloaded from the hosted OpenAI API, and the annotation data can be downloaded from the annotated videos within the HUMBI dataset. Despite the growing need for models in non-English languages, natural language processing has long been Anglo-centric, and translating neural models between languages can be costly and time-consuming in terms of data labeling, development time, and expertise. We propose a universal approach to effortlessly and effectively transfer neural models from English to other languages. Our method utilizes weak supervision in the form of task representations and can adapt pre-trained models with minimal labels by leveraging the similarities between tasks and languages. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by successfully transferring an English sentiment classifier to three foreign languages with outstanding results and minimal resource requirements. Furthermore, we show that our technique remains effective even when trained using weak labels and surpasses strong supervision methods in several sentiment analysis benchmarks. Ultimately, we argue that task representations offer a versatile solution for cross-lingual model transfer and can become a crucial tool in developing neural models for languages with limited data and resources. The code for this paper is available at https://github.com/jbarnesspain/uncertainty-guided-ensemble. (Note: This paper was originally published under the title 'Model Agnostic Cross-Lingual Transfer with Task Representations' at NeurIPS 2021.)

In multi-task reinforcement learning, using shared representations can greatly
benefit a learner when it comes to solving a variety of tasks. While this
synergy is evident in model-free methods using shared policy networks, our study
investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks, one for each task, significantly improves the learning process. We
also provide an analysis explaining why using a shared dynamics model can be
harmful and validate its potential against existing models in the field. Through
this research, we prove that model-based multi-task reinforcement learning is
possible and open the door for further exploration into the underlying causes. 
Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/robot-learning/mbt-ambt. 
This work was financially supported by ONR and NTL. For references see the document. 
It will be presented at IJCAI 2023.

This research proposes a probabilistic model for analyzing the impact of combined hurricane and storm surge events on large power grids. To simulate real-world hurricane scenarios, the study generates probabilistic storm paths based on historical data, and corresponding storm surge situations are developed based on actual hurricane parameters. To assess potential losses, the study employs a quantitative metric that estimates total load reduction, and these outcomes are calculated using a simulated model of the 2000-bus Texas power system superimposed onto an actual map of the region. Simulation results indicate that power substations experiencing storm surge-related flooding may incur additional losses as the hurricane continues to move inland. To confirm these findings, the study compares total load reduction with the actual energy consumption in Texas during a real hurricane event in 2017. The proposed model demonstrates its effectiveness in estimating power losses caused by real-world hurricane events, and its output can be utilized by utility companies to estimate potential power losses ahead of actual hurricane landfalls. Furthermore, this model may also inform emergency response planning for hurricane situations. To validate this analysis, the study also estimates and compares total power losses with and without consideration of actual power transmission lines. The results of this investigation indicate that power losses caused by hurricane events may be underestimated if transmission effects are not taken into account. Ultimately, this research establishes a foundation for further study into the combined impact of hurricanes and storm surges on power systems. To extend this investigation, the study analyzes the relationship between hurricane parameters and resulting power losses. Our proof relies on an examination of the quasilinearization of the Dirac operator, followed by a thorough analysis of the monotonicity of the Dirac operator's differential operator. Ultimately, this leads to a proof of the three balls theorem for eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator. Additionally, we include a novel monotonicity formula relevant to Clifford analysis. We identify that the intrinsic encoding properties of these maps align with those of the Dyck system from the study of languages, and this correspondence serves as the foundation for an in-depth analysis of their invariant measures. Through initial investigation, we confirm the existence of two distinct ergodic measures with maximal entropy for these generalized baker maps, and also reveal the underlying cause for the failure of certain entropy-based approaches. Furthermore, our study provides a new mechanism to explain this failure, and it potentially sheds light on the phenomenon of unstable dimension variability. We also explore the one-dimensional analogs of these generalized baker maps and establish a relationship with a class of piecewise affine transformations widely studied in ergodic theory. Additionally, we show that the ergodic measure with maximal entropy for these one-dimensional maps has an encoding property, denoted as the Dyck code, and this measure is unique under a specific condition. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the large number of parameters make WN prone to overfitting, which can be exacerbated by the excessive complexity of WB in modeling periodic signals. To overcome these challenges, QPNet is proposed to effectively capture the periodic characteristics of acoustic sources, specifically using a pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural network architecture. In addition to improving pitch control, this model also facilitates signal periodization. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed model surpasses WN in terms of performance and parameter efficiency, with a significant reduction in the number of parameters required. Notably, QPNet achieves superior quality and per-parameter log likelihood performance compared to WN+PDCNN, the state-of-the-art prior knowledge-based WN extension. Additionally, the model exhibits great potential for applications in low-bitrate audio coding and adversarial sampling methods. Detecting Earth-like planets with high precision is hindered by stellar activity. Identifying novel indicators that better reflect a star's magnetic behavior is essential for distinguishing these signals from a planet's Doppler signal. In this research, we studied the spectral features of stellar activity using data from the HARPS-N solar telescope, and found patterns distinct from a quiet star's spectrum. By comparing various activity indicators, we found that certain features are less affected by variations in temperature and pressure, and are better represented by a single parameter - the line-gas component of a star's spectrum. We proposed and tested this new indicator, which effectively tracks a star's magnetic behavior and distinguishes it from a planet's Doppler signal. This indicator has minimal interference from changes in temperature and pressure, and is highly correlated with ZDI data (.88), making it a reliable indicator of a star's magnetic behavior. However, using this indicator may introduce some biases in the recovery of M_E characteristics. Additionally, we found that using the widely used FWHM metric actually introduces noise that can mask a star's magnetic behavior and a planet's Doppler signal, leading to inaccurate results and false negatives. In contrast, using the new indicator avoids these limitations and allows for a more accurate characterization of a star's magnetic behavior and a planet's Doppler signal. We supported these findings with physical modeling, and provided an overview of how these indicators work along with their strengths and weaknesses. We also explored the potential of using these indicators to distinguish active and passive stellar noise, and found that using these indicators could improve harmonic removal and enhance the detection of Earth-like planets. Finally, we proposed and tested our idea with a simple approach called SII, which uses an unbiased estimator of a star's magnetic behavior and a planet's Doppler signal, and demonstrated its effectiveness with simulated data. Additionally, we conducted our research during the COVID-19 pandemic when data was not available, and thus could not include it in this research but expect it to improve our outcomes in the future. In summary, we presented novel indicators of stellar activity, and demonstrated their potential to distinguish a star's magnetic behavior from a planet's Doppler signal, and ultimately allow for the detection of Earth-like planets. These indicators are ready for use in current observations, and we expect to improve our results in the future with additional data. Measuring the spectral density of a Majorana zero mode at a point contact in a topological superconductor is difficult due to the limited understanding of hybridized modes. To overcome this challenge, we investigate a setup where a resistive material is used as one electrode in a tunneling experiment. Focusing on a model consisting of a resistive material with variable density and ohmic loss, we found that the tunneling current versus voltage (I-V) spectra provide distinct information about different modes near a Majorana zero mode. Specifically, non-local variations in resistance are indicative of a zero-bias peak caused by hybridized modes, whereas a local resistance peak near the zero-bias point is indicative of the Majorana zero mode itself. Furthermore, we observed that the tunneling current decays over time due to ohmic loss in the electrode, which is supported by theoretical predictions. Our study indicates that Ohmic Dissipation using Resistive Electrodes (ODRJE) offers a viable method for distinguishing between different modes near a Majorana zero mode through tunneling spectroscopy. This approach can serve as a crucial tool for accurately identifying Majorana zero modes. Additionally, we applied our understanding of ODRIE to a recent experiment involving a hybrid device consisting of a semiconductor and a superconductor. Our analysis predicts that the observed low-bias peak could be explained as a hybridized mode, which is consistent with the predicted spectral density for such a mode. This understanding could facilitate the identification of Majorana zero modes in various nanoscopic hybrid systems. Lastly, we proposed several theoretical modifications to distinguish between modes in such systems, including introducing a new type of q-body interaction and adjusting the hybridization strength to match anisotropic Kondo energies. These proposals could improve our understanding of different modes in nanoscopic systems. Additionally, we applied our theoretical analysis to a recent tunneling spectroscopy experiment on a Majorana mode, which suggests that the hybridized mode is responsible for the observed low-bias peak. This understanding could facilitate identifying Majorana zero modes in various nanoscopic systems. The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories with comonadic properties, it has been demonstrated that shadows can be expressed as a bicategorical extension of THH. Additionally, this relationship has been formulated in terms of bicategorical traces, resulting in a characterization of shadows as a manifestation of such traces. As a fundamental consequence, this connection ensures the existence of a homotopy invariant metric on the space of shadows, accurately reflecting Morita invariance. Moreover, this relationship enables a thorough comprehension of the properties of shadows, ultimately yielding a straightforward proof of the fact that shadows form a homotopy invariant metric space. Furthermore, this composition also yields a compositional proof of the fact that shadows exhibit a homotopy hypothesis, a concept that can be broadly generalized across various homotopy theories. Finally, this paper introduces a novel metric on the space of shadows, defined as the homotopy metric, demonstrating that it is equivalent to the standard metric and retaining the properties of homotopy invariance and the homotopy hypothesis. Additionally, this paper presents a range of illustrative examples highlighting the complex interplay between shadows and THH. Specifically, it shows that the homotopy theory of monoidal categories does not exhibit a homotopy hypothesis, yet displays a homotopy invariance. Conversely, it demonstrates that the homotopy theory of non-negative simplicial rings exhibits a homotopy hypothesis, yet fails to demonstrate a homotopy invariance. Lastly, this paper presents a range of open problems and promising areas for further investigation. Primarily, it poses the query of whether the space of shadows retains its homotopy invariance when generalized to the space of homotopy equivalent categories. Secondly, it presents the conjecture that the space of shadows formed from the monoidal category of superline arrangements, denoted as $\mathcal{SH}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{SL}})$, should be a perfect example exhibiting a homotopy hypothesis. Lastly, it presents the query of whether the space of shadows formed from the monoidal category of line arrangements, denoted as $\mathcal{SH}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{L}})$, should be a perfect example exhibiting a homotopy invariance. Existing approaches to image editing tasks like color grading often yield multiple possible outcomes rather than a single definitive result, as numerous different styles can produce similar visual content. Current machine learning-based methods typically disregard this stylistic variability in their pursuit of identifying unique characteristics. Conversely, our research aims to harness style-specific information, extracting it from image pairs to condense into a two or three-dimensional representation, thereby preserving the diverse range of stylistic tastes. To achieve this, we develop multiple novel components, including a forward-and-backward mapping network, self-supervised and contrastive loss functions, and a statistical descriptor capturing the temporal structure of image sequences. The resulting low-dimensional style representation enables generation of new content from a single image, allowing for seamless interaction and adaptation to various styles across multiple domains. Empirical evaluations confirm the distinct capture of multiple styles, as well as the ability to effectively encode the temporal context in images, as demonstrated through numerous qualitative and quantitative assessments. Notably, our method's style representation exhibits a notable correlation with the perceived aesthetic appeal, surpassing leading generative flow models. The proposed framework receives accolades for its ability to accurately capture the temporal structure and diverse range of stylistic tastes, outperforming prior art in numerous ways. This field research focuses on snow deposition dynamics by monitoring the atmosphere's flow patterns and snowflake trajectories in real time. A state-of-the-art, high-resolution imaging system is utilized to capture snowflakes in motion, mapping the flow patterns and detecting vortex formations above the ground. Concurrently, a high-resolution camera is employed to track individual snowflakes in a smaller sample area within the main field of view, revealing the connection between atmospheric turbulence and snowflake settling patterns. Our research reveals that as snowflakes interact with turbulence at critical velocities, their falling speed is greatly increased, a phenomenon not seen in prior studies. Images captured within the flow patterns show that snowflakes tend to concentrate near the base of vortex formations, moving preferentially downwards. This study provides the first empirical evidence of a speeding-up effect and the role of atmospheric turbulence in snow deposition processes. Additionally, preferential sweeping could be a key factor in snow settling patterns, influencing the distribution of larger particles settling behind smaller ones. Further analysis connects this phenomenon to the differentiating factors behind snow crystal formation and growth. Finally, the templates of settling particles could be used to improve models of snow deposition dynamics, a field closely tied to glaciology and understanding the Earth's climate. Utilizing these images, we have created a movie illustrating the accelerated settling of snowflakes and preferential sweeping. This research has a significant implication for snow settlement and can be a valuable resource for scientific studies in glaciology, snow cover forecasting, and climate modeling. Moving forward, we plan to conduct a comparative study in two locations, differing in atmospheric conditions, to broaden the research and explore its potential connections to global cryospheric processes. A fundamental theory known as active inference underpins how living beings interact with their surroundings. This theory views the brain as an efficient tool that employs Bayesian principles to create a detailed mental framework, aiming to minimize uncertainty about the world. Despite the theory's significance in cognitive neuroscience, its practical application is restricted to simplified simulations due to limitations in dealing with large and varied environments. This research incorporates the latest advancements in deep learning to create a more sophisticated mental framework, one that can be built directly from high-dimensional data, such as video feeds, without the need for pre-defined parameters. Furthermore, this work demonstrates that such frameworks can be utilized to facilitate active inference. This study marks the first instance of applying active inference using deep learning techniques to a real-world navigation task involving a robotic system. While still in its initial stages, this research shows that deep active inference can enable robots to create a mental context for making informed decisions, even in complex environments with limited computational resources. Experimental findings reveal that deep active inference navigates more efficiently and successfully compared to other methods. Nonetheless, results indicate that deep active inference sometimes leads to sub-optimal performance due to the slow convergence of the deep sampling algorithm. This has prompted the development of novel variants that leverage modern deep learning techniques, specifically the emergence of contrastive learning, to create a more agile mental context. This development enables faster and more robust decision-making, enhancing the overall performance and potentially paving the way for the deployment of active inference in real-world applications. New tests confirm that the advanced variants outperform other methods and demonstrate more resilient results. This work presents a new approach to active inference, one that uses contrastive learning to create a more dynamic and adaptable mental framework. While still a novel concept, this method shows great potential in tackling challenges within real-world navigation, particularly those involving multiple tasks and competing priorities. This research makes key contributions, especially in regards to the widespread applicability of active inference in practical scenarios. Optimizing wireless Device-to-Device (D2D) communication success depends heavily on minimizing excessive interference through effective device scheduling. Traditional scheduling methods mainly prioritize maximizing throughput and fairness without considering the timeliness of received data. This paper presents a novel D2D link scheduling strategy that balances both Age of Information (AoI) and throughput by employing a packet replacement policy, which ensures fair link activation. Analytically derived expressions demonstrate how the network's overall AoI and throughput are affected under complex spatio-temporal interference. Furthermore, a neural network is designed to learn an optimal mapping between geographical locations and scheduling parameters under a random policy, eliminating the need for Channel State Information (CSI) after training. Additionally, a novel method is proposed to back-propagate the loss through the network, which enables efficient learning. Experimental results show that the proposed neural network achieves near-optimal performance comparable to the local optimal algorithm with significantly lower computational requirements. This research provides key insights into the performance trade-off between data freshness and throughput in wireless D2D communications. Moreover, it indicates that deep learning can be leveraged to develop efficient algorithms for this context. An extension of this work to the case where D2D transmitters are powered by energy-harvesting (EH) sources is also considered, which introduces additional challenges due to the dependence of link availability on the transmitters' AoI. This problem is tackled using a similar deep learning approach, which is evaluated through comparative simulations. An important conclusion from these experiments is that the trained neural network can successfully generalize to the case where D2D transmitters employ energy-harvesting as their sole power source. This generalization capability proves that the developed scheduling strategy can effectively operate in communication systems powered by energy-harvesting technologies. An extension of this research to its theoretical framework is planned in the near future. Additionally, the efficiency of the proposed scheduling strategy, particularly its applicability to D2D systems utilizing frequency division duplex (FDD), will be explored further in the near future. It is anticipated that these findings will provide a solid theoretical foundation that can be utilized in real-world wireless communication systems. Real-life occurrences typically involve sudden changes in network behavior patterns. Current methods for dynamic node representations are ineffective at capturing event-driven network changes.  To address these limitations, we propose a new approach, called DyGED, for recognizing events in evolving networks using a combination of temporal self-attention and structural awareness.  Through extensive testing with diverse datasets, we demonstrate that DyGED consistently outperforms alternative methods in accuracy, achieving up to a 10% improvement.  Notably, it also offers improved scalability compared to the best-performing models, along with insightful case studies that highlight its key features.  To facilitate broad adoption, we have made the code for DyGED publicly available. The growing presence of artificial intelligence systems has led to a significant rise in the need for their explanations. Transparency and stakeholder trust are achieved by reducing the opacity of these systems through the provision of explanations. In this paper, we will explore the interconnection between explainable AI and requirements engineering. The challenges in the XAI field will be highlighted and solutions proposed, with a framework and future research directions on how requirements engineering can aid in addressing these difficulties. By adopting a user-centered approach to capturing explainability needs, requirements engineers can create data-driven, actionable strategies for developing explainable systems that meet the evolving demands of their stakeholders. This includes finding suitable XAI techniques, establishing measurable evaluation criteria, and creating adaptable solutions to accommodate shifting user requirements. This two-way approach will help bridge the gaps between explainability theory, AI development, and user needs, resulting in more practical solutions for real-world applications. With this, we aim to establish a foundation for integrating requirements engineering and EXAI and outline further study opportunities.
